Perimeter measures the distance around a shape; **[[area]]** measures the amount of surface inside it. Area is counted in **[[square units]]**: a square 1 cm on each side has an area of 1 square centimeter (1 cm²). To find an area is to count how many of these unit squares fit inside. This lesson builds the area formulas for the common polygons, each one from the one before, so you can rebuild any of them if you forget.

## Rectangles and squares

A rectangle 5 units long and 3 units wide holds 3 rows of 5 unit squares, or 15 squares in all.

```shape
{"polygons": [{"points": [[0, 0], [5, 0], [5, 3], [0, 3]]}], "segments": [{"from": [1, 0], "to": [1, 3]}, {"from": [2, 0], "to": [2, 3]}, {"from": [3, 0], "to": [3, 3]}, {"from": [4, 0], "to": [4, 3]}, {"from": [0, 1], "to": [5, 1]}, {"from": [0, 2], "to": [5, 2]}], "caption": "A 5 by 3 rectangle contains 15 unit squares"}
```

$$\text{Rectangle: } A = lw \qquad \text{Square: } A = s^2$$

The formula works for fractional and decimal sides too: a 2.5 m by 4 m rug covers 10 m².

## Parallelograms

A **[[parallelogram]]** is a quadrilateral whose opposite sides are parallel. Cut a right triangle off one end and slide it to the other end, and the parallelogram becomes a rectangle with the same base and the same height.

```shape
{"polygons": [{"points": [[0, 0], [6, 0], [8, 3], [2, 3]]}], "segments": [{"from": [2, 3], "to": [2, 0], "dashed": true, "label": "h"}, {"from": [0, -0.4], "to": [6, -0.4], "label": "b"}], "rightAngles": [[[2, 0], [3, 0], [2, 1]]], "caption": "A parallelogram with base b and height h"}
```

$$\text{Parallelogram: } A = bh$$

The **[[height]]** must be measured *perpendicular* to the base (the dashed line), not along the slanted side. The slanted side is longer than the height, and using it gives too big an area.

## Triangles

Two copies of any triangle fit together to make a parallelogram with the same base and height. So a triangle's area is half the parallelogram's:

$$\text{Triangle: } A = \tfrac12 bh$$

Again, the height is the perpendicular distance from the base to the opposite vertex. In a right triangle the two legs are a base and its height. In an obtuse triangle the height may fall outside the triangle.

### Example 1

Find the area of a triangle with base 14 cm and height 9 cm.

$A = \tfrac12(14)(9) = 63 \text{ cm}^2$.

### Example 2

A triangle has sides 13, 13 and 10 in, and its height to the 10-inch side is 12 in. Find the area and perimeter.

Area: $\tfrac12(10)(12) = 60 \text{ in}^2$. Perimeter: $13 + 13 + 10 = 36$ in. Notice that the 13-inch sides are not used for the area, and the height isn't used for the perimeter.

## Trapezoids

A **[[trapezoid]]** has exactly one pair of parallel sides, called the bases $b_1$ and $b_2$. The two sides that are not parallel are called its legs, and its height is the perpendicular distance between the bases.

![A trapezoid with a long horizontal base b₁ at the bottom, a shorter parallel base b₂ at the top, a dashed vertical height h with a right-angle mark, and a slanted side labeled leg.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Two copies of a trapezoid, one flipped, fit together to make a parallelogram with base $b_1 + b_2$ and the same height. Half of that is

$$\text{Trapezoid: } A = \tfrac12 (b_1 + b_2) h.$$

In words: the average of the two bases, times the height.

```shape
{"polygons": [{"points": [[0, 0], [9, 0], [7, 4], [2, 4]]}], "segments": [{"from": [0, -0.4], "to": [9, -0.4], "label": "b₁ = 9"}, {"from": [2, 4.4], "to": [7, 4.4], "label": "b₂ = 5"}, {"from": [2, 4], "to": [2, 0], "dashed": true, "label": "h = 4"}], "rightAngles": [[[2, 0], [3, 0], [2, 1]]], "caption": "Trapezoid with bases 9 and 5 and height 4"}
```

### Example 3

Find the area of the trapezoid in the figure.

$A = \tfrac12(9 + 5)(4) = \tfrac12(14)(4) = 28$ square units.

## Composite figures

Many real shapes are combinations of rectangles, triangles and trapezoids. Find the area by *splitting* the shape into simple pieces and adding, or by *subtracting* a missing piece from a larger shape.

This chart sums up which formula to reach for:

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  accTitle: Choosing an area formula
  accDescr: First ask what shape it is. A rectangle uses length times width, and a square side times side. A parallelogram uses base times perpendicular height. A triangle uses half of base times perpendicular height. A trapezoid uses half the sum of the two bases times the perpendicular height. Any other shape is split into these shapes, or a missing piece is subtracted from a larger shape.
  Q{"What shape is it?"}
  Q -- "rectangle or square" --> R["A = length × width (square: side × side)"]
  Q -- "parallelogram" --> P["A = base × perpendicular height"]
  Q -- "triangle" --> T["A = half of base × perpendicular height"]
  Q -- "trapezoid" --> Z["A = half of (b1 + b2) × perpendicular height"]
  Q -- "something else" --> C["Split it into these shapes, or subtract a missing piece"]
```

### Example 4

An L-shaped room is described by the figure. Find its floor area.

```shape
{"polygons": [{"points": [[0, 0], [12, 0], [12, 5], [5, 5], [5, 10], [0, 10]]}], "segments": [{"from": [0, -0.5], "to": [12, -0.5], "label": "12 ft"}, {"from": [12.5, 0], "to": [12.5, 5], "label": "5 ft"}, {"from": [-0.5, 0], "to": [-0.5, 10], "label": "10 ft"}, {"from": [0, 10.5], "to": [5, 10.5], "label": "5 ft"}, {"from": [5, 5], "to": [5, 0], "dashed": true}], "caption": "An L-shaped room"}
```

Split with the dashed line into a 5 ft by 10 ft rectangle on the left and a 7 ft by 5 ft rectangle on the right (the bottom is 12 ft, so the right part is $12 - 5 = 7$ ft wide).

$A = 5 \times 10 + 7 \times 5 = 50 + 35 = 85 \text{ ft}^2$.

Check by subtracting: the full 12 by 10 rectangle is 120 ft², and the missing top-right corner is $7 \times 5 = 35$ ft². $120 - 35 = 85$. ✓

### Example 5

Carpet costs \$4.25 per square foot. How much does it cost to carpet the room in Example 4?

$85 \times 4.25 = 361.25$, so \$361.25.

## Changing units of area

Recall from Lesson 30 that area units convert by the square of the length factor. A room of 85 ft² is $85 \div 9 \approx 9.44$ square yards, since 1 yd² = 9 ft².

## Area and perimeter are different

Two shapes with the same perimeter can have very different areas. A 1 ft by 11 ft rectangle and a 6 ft by 6 ft square both have perimeter 24 ft, but their areas are 11 ft² and 36 ft². Among rectangles with a given perimeter, the square has the largest area. Long, thin shapes have a lot of edge for very little inside.

### Example 6

A farmer has 40 m of fence for a rectangular pen. Compare a 5 m by 15 m pen with a 10 m by 10 m pen.

Both use $2(5) + 2(15) = 40$ m and $2(10) + 2(10) = 40$ m of fence. The areas are $5 \times 15 = 75$ m² and $10 \times 10 = 100$ m². The square pen encloses a third more ground with the same fence.

## Common mistakes

- *Using a slanted side as the height.* The height is always perpendicular to the base.
- *Forgetting the $\tfrac12$* for triangles and trapezoids.
- *Giving area in plain units.* Area is in square units: ft², cm², m².
- *Missing a hidden length* in a composite figure; find it from the lengths you know (like $12 - 5 = 7$).
- *Converting area with the length factor:* 1 yd² is 9 ft², not 3 ft².

## Key points

- Rectangle $A = lw$; square $A = s^2$; parallelogram $A = bh$.
- Triangle $A = \tfrac12 bh$; trapezoid $A = \tfrac12(b_1 + b_2)h$.
- Heights are perpendicular to the base.
- Composite figures: split into pieces and add, or subtract a missing piece.
- Area is measured in square units.

lessons.title: Circles
lessons.body:
## Round shapes

Wheels, pizzas, pipes, clocks and running tracks are all built on circles. Unlike polygons, circles have no straight sides, so their perimeter and area need a new ingredient: the number $\pi$. This lesson introduces the parts of a circle, where $\pi$ comes from, and the formulas for circumference and area.

## Parts of a circle

A **[[circle]]** is the set of all points in a plane at the same distance from a fixed point, its **[[center]]**.

- The **[[radius]]** $r$ is the distance from the center to the circle.
- The **[[diameter]]** $d$ is the distance across the circle through the center. It's two radii: $d = 2r$, so $r = \tfrac{d}{2}$.
- The **[[circumference]]** $C$ is the distance around the circle (its perimeter).

```shape
{"circles": [{"center": [0, 0], "r": 3}], "points": [[0, 0]], "segments": [{"from": [0, 0], "to": [2.12, 2.12], "label": "r"}, {"from": [-3, 0], "to": [3, 0], "label": "d"}], "caption": "Radius r and diameter d = 2r"}
```

Here are all four parts in one picture. The circumference is the curve itself, the edge all the way around.

![A circle with its center marked by a dot, a horizontal diameter d through the center, a radius r from the center to the edge, and the curved edge labeled circumference C.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

## Where π comes from

Wrap a string around any circular object, then compare its length to the diameter. A soup can, a bicycle wheel, a coin: the circumference is always a little more than 3 times the diameter. That ratio is the same for every circle, and it's called **[[pi]]** ($\pi$):

$$\pi = \frac{C}{d} \approx 3.14159\ldots$$

Pi is an irrational number: its decimal never ends or repeats. For calculations we use $\pi \approx 3.14$ or $\pi \approx \tfrac{22}{7}$, or the calculator's $\pi$ key. An answer left "in terms of $\pi$", like $10\pi$ cm, is exact.

## Circumference

Since $\dfrac{C}{d} = \pi$, multiplying by $d$ gives

$$C = \pi d = 2\pi r.$$

### Example 1

A bicycle wheel has a diameter of 26 inches. How far does the bike travel in one turn of the wheel? In 500 turns?

One turn: $C = \pi d = 26\pi \approx 81.7$ in. In 500 turns: $500 \times 81.68 \approx 40{,}841$ inches, which is about $40{,}841 \div 12 \approx 3{,}403$ feet.

### Example 2

A circular garden has a circumference of 44 m. What is its radius? (Use $\pi \approx \tfrac{22}{7}$.)

$C = 2\pi r$, so $44 = 2 \cdot \tfrac{22}{7} \cdot r = \tfrac{44}{7}r$. Multiply both sides by $\tfrac{7}{44}$: $r = 7$ m.

## Area

$$A = \pi r^2$$

Why? Cut a circle into many thin wedges like pizza slices and arrange them alternately point-up and point-down. They form a shape that is almost a parallelogram. Its height is the radius $r$, and its base is half the circumference (half the crust is on top, half on the bottom): $\tfrac12 \cdot 2\pi r = \pi r$. The more slices, the closer the shape is to a true parallelogram, with area base × height $= \pi r \cdot r = \pi r^2$.

![Left: a circle cut into 12 equal wedges, the top six shaded one color and the bottom six another. Right: the same wedges laid side by side, alternately pointing up and down, forming a shape that is almost a parallelogram with height r and a base of about half the circumference, πr, so its area is about πr times r, or πr².](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Be careful: the area formula uses the *radius*. If you're given the diameter, halve it first.

### Example 3

A pizza has a 14-inch diameter. Find its area.

The radius is 7 in. $A = \pi(7)^2 = 49\pi \approx 153.9 \text{ in}^2$.

### Example 4

Which is more pizza: one 16-inch pizza or two 10-inch pizzas?

One 16-inch: $\pi(8)^2 = 64\pi \approx 201 \text{ in}^2$. Two 10-inch: $2 \cdot \pi(5)^2 = 50\pi \approx 157 \text{ in}^2$. The single large pizza has about 28% more. Doubling a circle's radius multiplies its area by 4, because the radius is squared.

## Semicircles and composite shapes

A **[[semicircle]]** is half a circle: half the area, $\tfrac12 \pi r^2$. Its curved edge is half the circumference, $\pi r$.

### Example 5

A window is a 4 ft by 3 ft rectangle with a semicircle on top whose diameter is the 4 ft side. Find the window's area and its perimeter (the frame around the outside).

```shape
{"polygons": [{"points": [[0, 0], [4, 0], [4, 3], [0, 3]]}], "curves": [{"x": "2 + 2*cos(t)", "y": "3 + 2*sin(t)", "t": [0, "pi"]}], "segments": [{"from": [0, -0.4], "to": [4, -0.4], "label": "4 ft"}, {"from": [4.4, 0], "to": [4.4, 3], "label": "3 ft"}], "caption": "A rectangle topped by a semicircle"}
```

Area: rectangle $4 \times 3 = 12$; semicircle with radius 2: $\tfrac12\pi(2)^2 = 2\pi \approx 6.28$. Total $\approx 18.28 \text{ ft}^2$.

Perimeter: the bottom and two sides, $4 + 3 + 3 = 10$ ft, plus the curved top, $\pi r = 2\pi \approx 6.28$ ft. Total $\approx 16.28$ ft. The top edge of the rectangle is inside the window, so it isn't part of the perimeter.

## Working backward

Sometimes you know the area or circumference and need the radius. Undo the formula step by step.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: Finding the radius from what you know
  accDescr: If you know the diameter, halve it to get the radius. If you know the circumference, divide it by 2 pi. If you know the area, divide it by pi and then take the square root. Every path ends with the radius.
  Q{"What do you know?"}
  Q -- "diameter d" --> D["Halve it: r = d ÷ 2"]
  Q -- "circumference C" --> C["Divide by 2π: r = C ÷ (2π)"]
  Q -- "area A" --> A1["Divide by π"] --> A2["Take the square root"]
  D --> R["The radius r"]
  C --> R
  A2 --> R
```

### Example 6

A circular patio has an area of about 113 square feet. What is its radius, to the nearest foot?

$\pi r^2 = 113$, so $r^2 = 113 \div \pi \approx 35.97$. Then $r = \sqrt{35.97} \approx 6$ feet. Check: $\pi(6)^2 = 36\pi \approx 113.1$. ✓

For circumference, divide by $2\pi$ instead: a circle with circumference 50 cm has radius $50 \div (2\pi) \approx 7.96$ cm. Notice that the area problem needs a square root at the end, because the radius is squared in the area formula.

## Common mistakes

- *Using the diameter in $A = \pi r^2$.* Halve it first.
- *Mixing up the formulas.* Circumference ($2\pi r$) is a length; area ($\pi r^2$) has square units. The squared $r$ goes with square units.
- *Squaring before multiplying incorrectly:* $\pi r^2$ means $\pi \times (r^2)$, not $(\pi r)^2$.
- *Rounding $\pi$ too early* in a multi-step problem. Keep $\pi$ until the end.
- *Including interior edges* in the perimeter of a composite figure.

## Key points

- $d = 2r$.
- $\pi = C/d \approx 3.14159$, the same for every circle.
- Circumference $C = \pi d = 2\pi r$; area $A = \pi r^2$.
- Exact answers keep $\pi$ (like $49\pi$); approximate answers use 3.14 or a calculator.
- A semicircle has half the area and half the curved length of the full circle.

lessons.title: Volume and surface area
lessons.body:
## Into three dimensions

Area measures flat surfaces. Real objects (boxes, tanks, cans, rooms) take up space, and two new questions arise: how much do they hold, and how much material covers them? The first is **[[volume]]**, the second **[[surface area]]**. This lesson handles the solids you'll meet most often: rectangular boxes, cubes, cylinders, and a few others for reference.

## Volume

**[[Volume]]** measures the space inside a solid, in **[[cubic units]]**: a cube 1 cm on each edge has a volume of 1 cubic centimeter (1 cm³). Finding a volume means counting how many unit cubes fit inside.

## Rectangular prisms (boxes)

A **[[rectangular prism]]** is a box shape with length $l$, width $w$ and height $h$.

```shape
{"polygons": [{"points": [[0, 0], [4, 0], [4, 2], [0, 2]]}, {"points": [[0, 2], [4, 2], [5.2, 2.9], [1.2, 2.9]]}, {"points": [[4, 0], [5.2, 0.9], [5.2, 2.9], [4, 2]]}], "segments": [{"from": [0, -0.35], "to": [4, -0.35], "label": "l"}, {"from": [4.45, 0.0], "to": [5.65, 0.9], "label": "w"}, {"from": [-0.35, 0], "to": [-0.35, 2], "label": "h"}], "caption": "A rectangular prism with length l, width w and height h"}
```

Picture filling it in layers. The bottom layer holds $l \times w$ unit cubes (the area of the base), and there are $h$ layers. So

$$V = lwh.$$

For a **[[cube]]** with edge $s$, all three dimensions are equal: $V = s^3$. (That's where "cubed" comes from.)

More generally, for any **[[prism]]** (a solid with two identical parallel bases and straight sides), the volume is the area of the base times the height: $V = Bh$, where $B$ is the base area.

### Example 1

A fish tank is 30 in long, 12 in wide and 16 in high. What is its volume? One gallon is about 231 in³; about how many gallons does it hold?

$V = 30 \times 12 \times 16 = 5{,}760 \text{ in}^3$. In gallons: $5{,}760 \div 231 \approx 24.9$, so about 25 gallons.

## Cylinders

A **[[cylinder]]** is like a prism with circular bases. Its base area is $\pi r^2$, so

$$V = \pi r^2 h.$$

### Example 2

A can has a diameter of 8 cm and a height of 11 cm. Find its volume.

The radius is 4 cm. $V = \pi(4)^2(11) = 176\pi \approx 552.9 \text{ cm}^3$.

Since 1 cm³ = 1 mL, the can holds about 553 mL.

## Other solids (for reference)

| Solid | Volume |
|---|---|
| Cone, radius $r$, height $h$ | $V = \tfrac13 \pi r^2 h$ |
| Pyramid, base area $B$, height $h$ | $V = \tfrac13 Bh$ |
| Sphere, radius $r$ | $V = \tfrac43 \pi r^3$ |

A cone holds exactly one third of the cylinder with the same base and height, and a pyramid one third of the matching prism.

## Surface area

**[[Surface area]]** is the total area of all the outside faces of a solid: how much paper it would take to wrap it. It's an area, so it's measured in square units.

For a rectangular prism, there are six rectangular faces in three matching pairs: top and bottom ($l \times w$ each), front and back ($l \times h$), and two sides ($w \times h$). So

$$SA = 2lw + 2lh + 2wh.$$

A cube has six identical square faces: $SA = 6s^2$.

One way to see this is to unfold the box into a flat pattern called a **[[net]]**: six rectangles you can measure separately and add.

### Example 3

A shipping box is 20 in by 14 in by 10 in. How much cardboard covers its surface?

$SA = 2(20)(14) + 2(20)(10) + 2(14)(10) = 560 + 400 + 280 = 1{,}240 \text{ in}^2$.

### Example 4

Find the surface area of a cylinder with radius 3 ft and height 10 ft.

Unroll it: two circles (top and bottom), each $\pi r^2 = 9\pi$, and a rectangle whose width is the circumference $2\pi r = 6\pi$ and whose height is 10. The rectangle's area is $6\pi \times 10 = 60\pi$.

The picture shows why the rectangle is that wide: its long edge wrapped once around the circular base.

![Left: a cylinder with radius r and height h. Right: its net, a rectangle with a circle touching its top edge and another touching its bottom edge. Each circle has area πr². The rectangle's long side has length 2πr, the circumference, its short side is h, and its area is 2πr times h.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Total: $SA = 2\pi r^2 + 2\pi r h = 18\pi + 60\pi = 78\pi \approx 245 \text{ ft}^2$.

## Volume vs surface area vs perimeter

| Measure | What it tells you | Units |
|---|---|---|
| Perimeter | distance around a flat shape | ft, cm (length) |
| Area | flat surface inside a shape | ft², cm² (square) |
| Surface area | total outside area of a solid | ft², cm² (square) |
| Volume | space inside a solid | ft³, cm³ (cubic) |

Painting a wall uses area; fencing a yard uses perimeter; filling a pool uses volume; wrapping a gift uses surface area.

When a word problem doesn't say which one it wants, ask what is being measured:

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  accTitle: Choosing perimeter, area, surface area or volume
  accDescr: Ask what the problem measures. A distance around a flat shape, like fencing or a frame, is perimeter, in plain units. A flat surface, like carpet or paint on a wall, is area, in square units. The whole outside of a solid, like wrapping paper or the material in a box, is surface area, in square units. The space inside a solid, like water in a tank or sand in a sandbox, is volume, in cubic units.
  Q{"What is being measured?"}
  Q -- "distance around a flat shape" --> P["Perimeter: ft, cm"]
  Q -- "a flat surface" --> A["Area: ft², cm²"]
  Q -- "the whole outside of a solid" --> S["Surface area: ft², cm²"]
  Q -- "the space inside a solid" --> V["Volume: ft³, cm³"]
```

### Example 5

A sandbox is 6 ft by 4 ft and should be filled 1.5 ft deep. Sand is sold by the cubic yard. How many cubic yards are needed?

Volume: $6 \times 4 \times 1.5 = 36 \text{ ft}^3$. One cubic yard is $3 \times 3 \times 3 = 27 \text{ ft}^3$, so $36 \div 27 \approx 1.33$ yd³. If the supplier sells only whole or half cubic yards, buy 1.5 yd³ (1 yd³ would not be enough).

## Common mistakes

- *Using the diameter instead of the radius* in $\pi r^2 h$.
- *Confusing volume and surface area.* Volume is cubic units (how much it holds); surface area is square units (how much covers it).
- *Counting only three faces* of a box for surface area; there are six.
- *Converting cubic units with the length factor:* 1 yd³ = 27 ft³, not 3 ft³.
- *Mixing units* (feet and inches) in one formula.

## Key points

- Volume counts cubic units; prism $V = Bh$, box $V = lwh$, cube $V = s^3$, cylinder $V = \pi r^2 h$.
- Surface area adds the areas of all faces: box $SA = 2lw + 2lh + 2wh$, cube $SA = 6s^2$, cylinder $SA = 2\pi r^2 + 2\pi rh$.
- Volume is in cubic units, surface area in square units, perimeter in plain units.

lessons.title: The Pythagorean theorem
lessons.body:
## Distances you can't measure directly

How long a ladder reaches the window? How far is it across a rectangular field on the diagonal? What's the screen size of a TV that is 48 inches wide and 27 inches tall? All of these involve right triangles, and one theorem answers them all. It ties together squares and square roots (Lesson 20), equations (Module 7) and area (Lesson 32).

## Parts of a right triangle

In a right triangle, the two sides that form the right angle are the **[[legs]]**, usually called $a$ and $b$. The side opposite the right angle is the **[[hypotenuse]]**, $c$. The hypotenuse is always the longest side.

```shape
{"polygons": [{"points": [[0, 0], [4, 0], [4, 3]]}], "rightAngles": [[[4, 0], [0, 0], [4, 3]]], "segments": [{"from": [0, 0], "to": [4, 0], "label": "a = 4"}, {"from": [4, 0], "to": [4, 3], "label": "b = 3"}, {"from": [4, 3], "to": [0, 0], "label": "c = 5"}], "caption": "A right triangle with legs 3 and 4 and hypotenuse 5"}
```

## The theorem

The **[[Pythagorean theorem]]**: in a right triangle with legs $a$ and $b$ and hypotenuse $c$,

$$a^2 + b^2 = c^2.$$

In the triangle above, $3^2 + 4^2 = 9 + 16 = 25 = 5^2$. ✓

In terms of area: a square built on the hypotenuse has exactly the same area as the two squares built on the legs combined.

*Why it's true (one of many proofs).* Take four copies of the right triangle and arrange them inside a big square of side $a + b$, with their hypotenuses forming a tilted square of side $c$ in the middle. The big square's area is $(a + b)^2$. It's also the four triangles plus the middle square: $4 \cdot \tfrac12 ab + c^2 = 2ab + c^2$. Now rearrange the same four triangles in the big square as two $a \times b$ rectangles (each cut along its diagonal), leaving two squares uncovered, of areas $a^2$ and $b^2$. Both big squares have the same area and hold the same four triangles, so the uncovered areas are equal: $c^2 = a^2 + b^2$.

```shape
{"polygons": [{"points": [[0, 0], [7, 0], [7, 7], [0, 7]]}, {"points": [[9, 0], [16, 0], [16, 7], [9, 7]]}, {"points": [[0, 0], [3, 0], [0, 4]], "fill": true}, {"points": [[7, 0], [7, 3], [3, 0]], "fill": true}, {"points": [[7, 7], [4, 7], [7, 3]], "fill": true}, {"points": [[0, 7], [0, 4], [4, 7]], "fill": true}, {"points": [[12, 0], [16, 0], [16, 3]], "fill": true}, {"points": [[12, 0], [12, 3], [16, 3]], "fill": true}, {"points": [[9, 3], [12, 3], [12, 7]], "fill": true}, {"points": [[9, 3], [9, 7], [12, 7]], "fill": true}], "segments": [{"from": [0, -0.5], "to": [3, -0.5], "label": "a"}, {"from": [3, -0.5], "to": [7, -0.5], "label": "b"}, {"from": [9, -0.5], "to": [12, -0.5], "label": "a"}, {"from": [12, -0.5], "to": [16, -0.5], "label": "b"}], "labels": [{"at": [3.5, 3.5], "text": "c²"}, {"at": [10.5, 1.5], "text": "a²"}, {"at": [14, 5], "text": "b²"}], "caption": "The same four right triangles (legs a and b, hypotenuse c) in two squares of side a + b. Left: the uncovered area is c². Right: it is a² + b²."}
```

The theorem works only for *right* triangles. For other triangles, $a^2 + b^2 \ne c^2$.

## Finding the hypotenuse

### Example 1

A rectangular field is 60 m by 80 m. How long is the diagonal path across it?

The diagonal is the hypotenuse of a right triangle with legs 60 and 80.

$c^2 = 60^2 + 80^2 = 3{,}600 + 6{,}400 = 10{,}000$, so $c = \sqrt{10{,}000} = 100$ m.

### Example 2

Find the hypotenuse of a right triangle with legs 5 and 9, to the nearest tenth.

$c^2 = 25 + 81 = 106$, so $c = \sqrt{106} \approx 10.3$. (Check the estimate: $10^2 = 100$ and $11^2 = 121$, so it should be a bit over 10. ✓)

## Finding a leg

If you know the hypotenuse and one leg, subtract:

$$a^2 = c^2 - b^2.$$

### Example 3

A 13-foot ladder leans against a wall with its foot 5 feet from the wall. How high up the wall does it reach?

```shape
{"polygons": [{"points": [[0, 0], [5, 0], [0, 12]]}], "rightAngles": [[[0, 0], [5, 0], [0, 12]]], "segments": [{"from": [0, 0], "to": [5, 0], "label": "5 ft"}, {"from": [5, 0], "to": [0, 12], "label": "13 ft"}, {"from": [0, 0], "to": [0, 12], "label": "h"}], "caption": "A ladder against a wall"}
```

The ladder is the hypotenuse. $h^2 = 13^2 - 5^2 = 169 - 25 = 144$, so $h = 12$ ft.

A very common mistake is adding $13^2 + 5^2$ here. Ask "which side is across from the right angle?" That one is $c$, and it must be the largest.

This chart keeps the two cases straight:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: Finding a missing side of a right triangle
  accDescr: Find the right angle. The side across from it is the hypotenuse c. If c is the unknown side, add the squares of the legs and take the square root. If a leg is unknown, subtract the square of the known leg from the square of c and take the square root. Either way, check that c is the longest side.
  A["Find the right angle"] --> B["The side across from it is the hypotenuse c"]
  B --> Q{"Is c the unknown side?"}
  Q -- "Yes" --> H["Add: c² = a² + b², then take the square root"]
  Q -- "No, a leg is unknown" --> L["Subtract: a² = c² − b², then take the square root"]
  H --> K["Check: c is the longest side"]
  L --> K
```

## Pythagorean triples

Sets of whole numbers that fit the theorem are called **[[Pythagorean triples]]**. The most common are

$$3, 4, 5 \qquad 5, 12, 13 \qquad 8, 15, 17 \qquad 7, 24, 25$$

Multiples work too: 6, 8, 10 and 9, 12, 15 come from 3, 4, 5. Recognizing these saves time.

## Testing for a right angle

The converse is also true: if the sides of a triangle satisfy $a^2 + b^2 = c^2$ (with $c$ the longest), the triangle is a right triangle. Builders use this to check square corners: mark 3 ft along one wall and 4 ft along the other; if the marks are 5 ft apart, the corner is square.

### Example 4

Is a triangle with sides 7, 10 and 12 a right triangle?

Longest side 12: $7^2 + 10^2 = 49 + 100 = 149$, but $12^2 = 144$. Not equal, so no.

### Example 5

A TV screen is 48 in wide and 27 in tall. Screen sizes are given by the diagonal. What size is it?

$c^2 = 48^2 + 27^2 = 2{,}304 + 729 = 3{,}033$, so $c = \sqrt{3{,}033} \approx 55.1$ in: a "55-inch" TV.

## Distance on a grid

The theorem also measures straight-line distance between two points on a grid. The grid here is the coordinate plane from Lesson 29: a horizontal number line (the $x$-axis) and a vertical one (the $y$-axis) that cross at 0, a point called the origin. Every point is named by an ordered pair $(x, y)$: the first number says how far to move left or right from the origin, the second how far to move up or down. Order matters: $(1, 2)$ and $(2, 1)$ are different points. The axes split the plane into four regions called quadrants; points with negative coordinates, like $(-3, 4)$, sit left of or below the origin.

To go from $(1, 2)$ to $(7, 10)$, you move 6 units across and 8 units up. Those moves are the legs of a right triangle, and the straight-line distance is the hypotenuse:

$$d = \sqrt{6^2 + 8^2} = \sqrt{36 + 64} = \sqrt{100} = 10.$$

```plot
{"x": [0, 9], "y": [0, 12], "equal": true, "points": [{"at": [1, 2], "label": "(1, 2)"}, {"at": [7, 10], "label": "(7, 10)"}], "segments": [{"from": [1, 2], "to": [7, 2], "dashed": true, "label": "6"}, {"from": [7, 2], "to": [7, 10], "dashed": true, "label": "8"}, {"from": [1, 2], "to": [7, 10], "label": "10"}], "caption": "The distance between two points is the hypotenuse of a right triangle"}
```

With negative coordinates, find each move by subtracting (Lesson 7) and ignore the sign, since a length is never negative. From $(-2, 3)$ to $(2, 0)$ the move across is $2 - (-2) = 4$ units and the move down is $3 - 0 = 3$ units, so the distance is $\sqrt{4^2 + 3^2} = \sqrt{25} = 5$.

In algebra this becomes the distance formula, but it is nothing more than the Pythagorean theorem.

## Common mistakes

- *Adding when you should subtract.* If the hypotenuse is given, $a^2 = c^2 - b^2$.
- *Forgetting the square root at the end:* $c^2 = 100$ means $c = 10$, not 100.
- *Writing $a + b = c$* or $\sqrt{a^2 + b^2} = a + b$. The square root does not split across addition.
- *Using the theorem on a triangle that isn't a right triangle.*
- *Calling a leg the hypotenuse.* The hypotenuse is opposite the right angle and is always longest.

## Key points

- In a right triangle, $a^2 + b^2 = c^2$, where $c$ is the hypotenuse (opposite the right angle).
- Hypotenuse: $c = \sqrt{a^2 + b^2}$. Leg: $a = \sqrt{c^2 - b^2}$.
- Common triples: 3-4-5, 5-12-13, 8-15-17, 7-24-25, and their multiples.
- If $a^2 + b^2 = c^2$ for a triangle's sides, it's a right triangle.
- The distance between two points on the coordinate plane is the hypotenuse of a right triangle whose legs are the moves across and up or down.

lessons.title: Angles of polygons and tilings
lessons.body:
## From triangles to every polygon

Lesson 31 proved that the angles of any triangle add to 180° and named the polygons: quadrilaterals, pentagons, hexagons, octagons. It also mentioned in passing that a quadrilateral's angles add to 360°. This lesson explains where that 360° comes from and finds the angle sum of *every* polygon, using nothing but the triangle fact. Then it uses the result to answer a practical question with a surprisingly short answer: which regular polygons can tile a floor with no gaps? Only three of them can, and you'll be able to prove it.

Throughout, $n$ stands for the number of sides of a polygon. A polygon has as many corners (vertices) as sides.

## Cutting a polygon into triangles

A **[[diagonal]]** of a polygon is a segment joining two vertices that are not next to each other. (A segment joining neighbors is a side.)

The angles inside a polygon, one at each vertex, are its **[[interior angles]]**. In this lesson the polygons are **[[convex]]**: every interior angle is less than 180°, so the polygon has no dents, and every diagonal lies inside it.

Pick one vertex of a convex polygon and draw every diagonal from it. The vertex can't connect to itself or its two neighbors, so there are $n - 3$ diagonals, and they cut the polygon into $n - 2$ triangles.

![A regular hexagon with three dashed diagonals drawn from its left vertex, cutting it into four numbered triangles. The caption reads: diagonals from one vertex, 4 triangles, 4 × 180° = 720°.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

The triangles' angles together make up exactly the polygon's interior angles: every triangle corner sits at a vertex of the polygon, and wherever two or more triangles share a vertex (the chosen vertex, and the far end of each diagonal), their corners fit side by side to make up that vertex's whole interior angle. Each triangle contributes 180°, so

$$\text{sum of interior angles} = (n - 2) \times 180°.$$

| Polygon | $n$ | Triangles | Angle sum |
|---|---|---|---|
| triangle | 3 | 1 | 180° |
| quadrilateral | 4 | 2 | 360° |
| pentagon | 5 | 3 | 540° |
| hexagon | 6 | 4 | 720° |
| octagon | 8 | 6 | 1,080° |
| decagon | 10 | 8 | 1,440° |

The formula also holds for polygons with dents (non-convex ones), but the proof needs a little more care, since a diagonal can then pass outside the polygon. We stick to convex polygons here.

### Example 1

Find the sum of the interior angles of a 12-sided polygon (a dodecagon).

$(12 - 2) \times 180° = 10 \times 180° = 1{,}800°$.

### Example 2

Four of the angles of a pentagon measure 100°, 110°, 120° and 95°. Find the fifth.

A pentagon's angles add to $(5 - 2) \times 180° = 540°$. The four known angles total $100 + 110 + 120 + 95 = 425°$, so the fifth is $540° - 425° = 115°$.

## Regular polygons

In a regular polygon all $n$ interior angles are equal (Lesson 31), so each one is the sum divided by $n$:

$$\text{each interior angle of a regular polygon} = \frac{(n - 2) \times 180°}{n}.$$

### Example 3

Find each interior angle of a regular hexagon and of a regular decagon.

Hexagon: $\dfrac{4 \times 180°}{6} = \dfrac{720°}{6} = 120°$. Decagon: $\dfrac{8 \times 180°}{10} = \dfrac{1{,}440°}{10} = 144°$.

As $n$ grows, the angles get closer and closer to 180° without reaching it: a regular polygon with many sides looks almost like a circle.

### Example 4

Each interior angle of a regular polygon is 150°. How many sides does it have?

Set up the equation and solve, as in Module 7: $\dfrac{(n - 2) \cdot 180}{n} = 150$. Multiply both sides by $n$: $180n - 360 = 150n$. Subtract $150n$ and add 360: $30n = 360$, so $n = 12$. (The next section gives a quicker way.)

## Exterior angles

Extend one side of a polygon past a vertex. The angle between the extension and the next side is an **[[exterior angle]]**. An interior angle and its exterior angle together form a straight angle, so they are supplementary:

$$\text{exterior angle} = 180° - \text{interior angle}.$$

![A regular pentagon with its bottom side extended to the right. An arc marks the interior angle at the bottom-left vertex, another arc marks the exterior angle at the bottom-right vertex between the extension and the next side, a dashed segment joins two vertices that are not neighbors (a diagonal), and one side is labeled side.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Here is the remarkable fact: *for any convex polygon, the exterior angles (one at each vertex) add to 360°*, however many sides it has.

*Why?* Imagine walking around the polygon's edge. At each corner you turn left by that corner's exterior angle. When you get back to the start you are facing the way you began, having turned around exactly once: 360°.

The algebra agrees. The $n$ straight angles at the vertices total $n \times 180°$. Take away the interior angles, $(n - 2) \times 180°$, and what's left is $n \times 180° - (n - 2) \times 180° = 2 \times 180° = 360°$.

For a regular polygon, all exterior angles are equal, so each is $\dfrac{360°}{n}$. This gives the quick route.

### Example 5

Redo Example 4 with exterior angles.

The exterior angle is $180° - 150° = 30°$. They total 360°, so there are $360 \div 30 = 12$ of them: 12 sides.

And going forward: a regular octagon has exterior angles of $360° \div 8 = 45°$, so each interior angle is $180° - 45° = 135°$. That matches $\tfrac{6 \times 180°}{8} = 135°$.

## Which regular polygons tile a floor?

A **[[tessellation]]** (or tiling) covers a flat surface with shapes that leave no gaps and don't overlap, like floor tiles. Suppose we tile using copies of a single regular polygon, meeting corner to corner. Where tiles meet, their angles must fill the full turn around the point exactly: they must add to 360°. So the interior angle must divide 360° a whole number of times.

- Equilateral triangles: 60°, and $360 \div 60 = 6$. Six triangles meet at each point. ✓
- Squares: 90°, and $360 \div 90 = 4$. ✓
- Regular pentagons: 108°, and $360 \div 108 \approx 3.33$. Three leave a 36° gap; four would overlap. ✗
- Regular hexagons: 120°, and $360 \div 120 = 3$. ✓
- Any regular polygon with more than 6 sides: its angle is more than 120° but less than 180°. Two of them make less than 360° and three make more than 360°. ✗

So there are exactly *three* regular tilings: triangles, squares and hexagons. Tilings that mix different regular polygons are possible too; the same rule (angles at each point add to 360°) rules out the mixtures that can't work. Passing the test at one point doesn't by itself guarantee that the pattern can be continued across a whole floor, but it is the first check.

![Left: a patch of a tiling by regular hexagons, three meeting at each point, with 120° + 120° + 120° = 360°. Right: a tiling by regular octagons with small squares in the gaps; two octagons and one square meet at each point, with 135° + 135° + 90° = 360°.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

### Example 6

Can two regular octagons and one square fit together around a point? Can three regular pentagons?

Octagons and square: $135° + 135° + 90° = 360°$. Yes; this is a common bathroom-floor pattern. Pentagons: $3 \times 108° = 324° < 360°$. No: a 36° gap is left.

### A note on honeycombs

Honeybees build their combs from hexagonal cells. A common explanation is that hexagons save wax: among the three regular tilings, hexagons enclose a given area with the least total wall length. In 1999 (published in 2001) the mathematician Thomas Hales proved a stronger statement, long known as the honeycomb conjecture: of *all* ways to divide a flat surface into regions of equal area, the regular hexagon pattern uses the least total boundary. (How bees actually come to build hexagons is still studied by biologists; the math explains why the shape is efficient, not how bees achieve it.)

## Common mistakes

- *Using $n \times 180°$ instead of $(n - 2) \times 180°$.* A triangle ($n = 3$) would then have 540°. Test your formula on a triangle.
- *Forgetting to divide by $n$* when asked for one angle of a regular polygon.
- *Dividing by $n$ for a polygon that isn't regular.* Only regular polygons have equal angles.
- *Mixing up interior and exterior angles.* They add to 180° at each vertex; the exterior angles of the whole polygon add to 360°.
- *Thinking the exterior angle sum grows with $n$.* It's always 360° for a convex polygon.
- *Assuming any regular polygon tiles.* The interior angle must divide 360° exactly.

## Key points

- From one vertex, $n - 3$ diagonals split a convex $n$-sided polygon into $n - 2$ triangles.
- Interior angle sum: $(n - 2) \times 180°$. Regular polygon: each angle $\tfrac{(n - 2) \times 180°}{n}$.
- Exterior angle $= 180° -$ interior angle. The exterior angles of a convex polygon add to 360°; for a regular polygon each is $\tfrac{360°}{n}$.
- To find $n$ for a regular polygon, divide 360° by its exterior angle.
- Angles meeting at a point of a tiling add to 360°; the only regular polygons that tile alone are the triangle, square and hexagon.

lessons.title: Pyramids, cones and spheres
lessons.body:
## Pointed and round solids

Lesson 34 listed the volume formulas for cones, pyramids and spheres "for reference." This lesson explains where they come from, why a third appears in two of them, and how to find the surface areas of these solids, which needs the Pythagorean theorem from Lesson 35. It ends with one of the most famous results in ancient mathematics: Archimedes' discovery of how a sphere compares with the cylinder that just holds it.

## The parts

A **[[pyramid]]** has a polygon for a base and triangular faces that meet at a single point, the **[[apex]]**. A square pyramid has a square base and four triangular faces. A **[[cone]]** is the round version: a circular base and a curved surface that narrows to an apex. (In this lesson, the apex sits directly above the center of the base: a *right* cone or pyramid.)

Two different "heights" matter, and mixing them up is the most common error with these solids:

- the height $h$ is the *perpendicular* distance from the apex straight down to the base;
- the **[[slant height]]** $\ell$ is measured along the slanted surface: for a cone, from the apex to the edge of the base; for a pyramid, from the apex down the middle of a triangular face to the base edge.

![A cone with its apex at the top, a dashed vertical height h from the apex to the center of the circular base, a radius r from the center to the edge of the base, a right-angle mark where they meet, and the slanted side labeled slant height ℓ.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Volume uses the height $h$. Surface area uses the slant height $\ell$.

## Volume: why one third?

A prism or cylinder has volume $V = Bh$ (base area times height). A pyramid or cone with the same base and height holds exactly one third as much:

$$\text{Pyramid: } V = \tfrac13 Bh \qquad \text{Cone: } V = \tfrac13 \pi r^2 h$$

There is a neat way to see the one third for one special pyramid. A cube with edge $s$ can be cut into three identical square pyramids. Each one has a face of the cube as its base and the same corner of the cube as its apex (the corner that doesn't touch any of those three faces). The three pyramids are identical and fill the cube, so each has volume $\tfrac13 s^3$, and $\tfrac13 s^3 = \tfrac13 (s^2)(s) = \tfrac13 Bh$. (These three pyramids are not *right* pyramids: each apex sits above a corner of its base, not its center. The height is still the perpendicular distance from the apex to the base, $s$.)

To get from this one pyramid to all pyramids and cones, mathematicians use **[[Cavalieri's principle]]**: if two solids have the same height, and every horizontal slice through them at the same level has the same area, then they have the same volume. (Think of a stack of coins: push it so it leans, and its volume doesn't change.) Every pyramid or cone with base area $B$ and height $h$ has slices that shrink in the same way from $B$ at the bottom to 0 at the apex, so they all have the same volume, $\tfrac13 Bh$. The full argument is a topic for geometry and calculus courses; here we accept the result. You can also test it with water: a cone-shaped cup filled three times fills a cylinder with the same base and height.

### Example 1

A paper cone cup has radius 3 cm and height 4 cm. How much water does it hold?

$V = \tfrac13 \pi r^2 h = \tfrac13 \pi (3)^2 (4) = \tfrac13 \pi (36) = 12\pi \approx 37.7$ cm³, about 38 mL.

### Example 2

The Great Pyramid of Giza originally had a square base about 230 m on a side and a height of about 147 m. Estimate its volume.

$V = \tfrac13 Bh \approx \tfrac13 (230^2)(147) = \tfrac13(52{,}900)(147) \approx 2{,}592{,}000$ m³. Its volume is usually given as about 2.6 million cubic meters, so the estimate agrees.

## Slant height and the Pythagorean theorem

Slice a cone straight down through its apex and the middle of its base. The cut shows a right triangle: the height $h$ and the radius $r$ are the legs, and the slant height $\ell$ is the hypotenuse. So

$$\ell^2 = r^2 + h^2.$$

For a square pyramid with base side $s$, the right triangle runs from the apex straight down to the center of the base, then out to the middle of a base edge, which is half a side away. Its legs are $h$ and $\tfrac{s}{2}$:

$$\ell^2 = h^2 + \left(\tfrac{s}{2}\right)^2.$$

### Example 3

A cone has radius 5 cm and height 12 cm. Find its slant height.

$\ell^2 = 5^2 + 12^2 = 25 + 144 = 169$, so $\ell = 13$ cm (a 5-12-13 triple).

### Example 4

A square pyramid has base side 6 m and height 4 m. Find the slant height of each face.

Half the base side is 3 m. $\ell^2 = 4^2 + 3^2 = 25$, so $\ell = 5$ m.

## Surface area

*Pyramid.* Add the base and the triangular faces. Each face of a square pyramid is a triangle with base $s$ and height $\ell$ (the slant height *is* the triangle's height), so

$$SA = s^2 + 4 \cdot \tfrac12 s\ell = s^2 + 2s\ell.$$

*Cone.* The base is a circle, $\pi r^2$. The curved part, called the **[[lateral surface]]**, unrolls into a fan shape: a slice of a circle of radius $\ell$ whose curved edge has length $2\pi r$ (it wrapped around the base). A full circle of radius $\ell$ would have area $\pi \ell^2$ and edge $2\pi \ell$; our slice has $\tfrac{2\pi r}{2\pi \ell} = \tfrac{r}{\ell}$ of that edge, so it has $\tfrac{r}{\ell}$ of that area: $\tfrac{r}{\ell} \cdot \pi \ell^2 = \pi r \ell$. So

$$\text{lateral area} = \pi r \ell, \qquad SA = \pi r^2 + \pi r \ell.$$

### Example 5

Find the surface areas of the cone in Example 3 and the pyramid in Example 4.

Cone: $SA = \pi(5)^2 + \pi(5)(13) = 25\pi + 65\pi = 90\pi \approx 282.7$ cm².

Pyramid: $SA = 6^2 + 2(6)(5) = 36 + 60 = 96$ m².

Notice that both used the slant height, not the height. Using $h = 12$ in the cone would give $25\pi + 60\pi = 85\pi$, which is wrong.

## Spheres

A **[[sphere]]** is the set of all points in space at the same distance $r$ from a center: the surface of a ball. Its formulas are

$$V = \tfrac43 \pi r^3, \qquad SA = 4\pi r^2.$$

Volume has $r^3$ (cubic units) and surface area $r^2$ (square units): doubling the radius multiplies the volume by 8 and the surface area by 4. Half a sphere is a **[[hemisphere]]**: half the volume, $\tfrac23 \pi r^3$, and a curved surface of $2\pi r^2$ (plus a flat circle of $\pi r^2$ if it is closed).

### Archimedes' sphere and cylinder

In the 200s BC, the Greek mathematician Archimedes of Syracuse compared a sphere with the cylinder that fits around it exactly: radius $r$ and height $2r$.

```shape
{"polygons": [{"points": [[-3, -3], [3, -3], [3, 3], [-3, 3]]}], "circles": [{"center": [0, 0], "r": 3}], "points": [[0, 0]], "segments": [{"from": [0, 0], "to": [3, 0], "label": "r"}, {"from": [3.5, -3], "to": [3.5, 3], "label": "2r"}], "caption": "Side view of a sphere of radius r inside a cylinder of radius r and height 2r"}
```

- The cylinder's volume is $\pi r^2 (2r) = 2\pi r^3$. The sphere's is $\tfrac43 \pi r^3$, which is exactly $\tfrac23$ of it.
- The cylinder's curved surface is $2\pi r \cdot 2r = 4\pi r^2$, exactly the sphere's surface area.
- A cone with the same base and height has volume $\tfrac13 \pi r^2(2r) = \tfrac23 \pi r^3$. So cone : sphere : cylinder $= \tfrac23 : \tfrac43 : 2 = 1 : 2 : 3$.

Archimedes was so proud of this result that, according to the Roman writer Cicero, his tomb was marked with a sphere inside a cylinder; Cicero wrote that he found the overgrown tomb in Syracuse more than a century later.

### Example 6

A basketball has a diameter of about 24 cm. Find its volume and surface area.

$r = 12$ cm. $V = \tfrac43 \pi (12)^3 = \tfrac43 \pi (1{,}728) = 2{,}304\pi \approx 7{,}238$ cm³, a little over 7 liters. $SA = 4\pi(12)^2 = 576\pi \approx 1{,}810$ cm².

### Example 7

A grain silo is a cylinder of radius 3 m and height 10 m with a hemisphere on top. How much does it hold?

Cylinder: $\pi(3)^2(10) = 90\pi$. Hemisphere: $\tfrac23 \pi (3)^3 = 18\pi$. Total $108\pi \approx 339.3$ m³. Keep $\pi$ until the end so the pieces add exactly.

## Common mistakes

- *Using the slant height for volume, or the height for surface area.* Volume uses $h$; lateral area uses $\ell$.
- *Forgetting the $\tfrac13$* for pyramids and cones.
- *Using the diameter* in place of the radius, especially in $\tfrac43\pi r^3$, where the error is multiplied by 8.
- *Squaring instead of cubing.* Sphere volume has $r^3$; sphere surface area has $r^2$.
- *Using the full base side* in the pyramid's slant-height triangle. The leg is half the side, $\tfrac{s}{2}$.
- *Forgetting the base* in a total surface area, or including it when the problem is about an open shape like an ice-cream cone.

## Key points

- Pyramid $V = \tfrac13 Bh$; cone $V = \tfrac13 \pi r^2 h$: one third of the matching prism or cylinder.
- Slant height by the Pythagorean theorem: cone $\ell^2 = r^2 + h^2$; square pyramid $\ell^2 = h^2 + (\tfrac s2)^2$.
- Square pyramid $SA = s^2 + 2s\ell$; cone $SA = \pi r^2 + \pi r\ell$.
- Sphere $V = \tfrac43 \pi r^3$, $SA = 4\pi r^2$; hemisphere half the volume.
- Archimedes: a sphere is $\tfrac23$ of its surrounding cylinder, and cone : sphere : cylinder $= 1 : 2 : 3$.

lessons.title: Precision and measurement error
lessons.body:
## Every measurement is rounded

In this module's lessons, a fish tank was "30 in" long and a can was "11 cm" tall, and we computed with those numbers as if they were exact. Real measurements never are. A ruler marked in centimeters can't tell 7 cm from 7.2 cm; a bathroom scale that shows whole pounds can't tell 150 lb from 150.4 lb. This lesson shows how to say exactly how uncertain a measurement is, how to compare that uncertainty with the size of the measurement, and what happens to it when measurements are multiplied to find areas and volumes. Scientists and engineers deal with these questions every day; the ideas here are their starting point.

## Precision and greatest possible error

The **[[precision]]** of a measurement is the size of the unit it was rounded to. "7 cm, measured to the nearest centimeter" has a precision of 1 cm; "7.2 cm, to the nearest tenth of a centimeter" has a precision of 0.1 cm, which is more precise.

When you round to the nearest unit, the true value can be off by up to half a unit in either direction. That half-unit is called the **[[greatest possible error]]** (GPE):

$$\text{greatest possible error} = \tfrac12 \times \text{precision}.$$

![A ruler marked from 0 to 10 cm with half-centimeter ticks. A bar above it ends a little past 7, so measured to the nearest centimeter it reads 7 cm. A shaded box over the ruler from 6.5 to 7.5 cm shows every true length that would also be read as 7 cm.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

So "7 cm to the nearest cm" means the true length is at least 6.5 cm and less than 7.5 cm. These two values are the **[[lower bound]]** and the **[[upper bound]]** of the measurement. With the rounding rule this course uses (ties round up), a true length of exactly 6.5 cm would read as 7 cm, but exactly 7.5 cm would read as 8 cm, so

$$6.5 \le L < 7.5.$$

```numberline
{"x": [6, 8], "points": [{"at": [6.5, 0], "label": "6.5"}, {"at": [7.5, 0], "open": true, "label": "7.5"}, {"at": [7, 0], "label": "7"}], "segments": [{"from": [6.5, 0], "to": [7.5, 0]}], "caption": "Every length from 6.5 up to (not including) 7.5 rounds to 7"}
```

In practice the difference between "less than 7.5" and "at most 7.5" rarely matters, and many books simply write $7 \pm 0.5$ cm. The bounds are what matter.

### Example 1

Find the greatest possible error and the bounds for each measurement.

| Measurement | Precision | GPE | Bounds |
|---|---|---|---|
| 3.2 kg, to the nearest 0.1 kg | 0.1 kg | 0.05 kg | 3.15 kg to 3.25 kg |
| 4,300 m, to the nearest 100 m | 100 m | 50 m | 4,250 m to 4,350 m |
| $5\tfrac12$ in, to the nearest $\tfrac14$ in | $\tfrac14$ in | $\tfrac18$ in | $5\tfrac38$ in to $5\tfrac58$ in |
| 12.00 s, to the nearest hundredth | 0.01 s | 0.005 s | 11.995 s to 12.005 s |

The last row shows why trailing zeros matter in measurements: "12.00 s" says more than "12 s". It claims precision to the hundredth of a second, so its bounds are 11.995 and 12.005, not 11.5 and 12.5.

## Precision is not accuracy

**[[Accuracy]]** is how close a measurement is to the true value. Precision is how finely it's reported. They are different things. A kitchen scale that reads to 0.1 g but was never zeroed (it shows 3.0 g with nothing on it) is precise but not accurate: every reading is about 3 g too high. A rough estimate of "about 200 m" for a 205 m path is accurate but not very precise.

(In science you will also see "precision" used for how close *repeated* measurements are to each other. Both meanings are about fineness and consistency, not about closeness to the truth.)

## Relative error

An error of 0.5 cm is huge when measuring a 2 cm beetle and tiny when measuring a 250 cm doorway. To compare, divide the error by the size of the measurement. The **[[relative error]]** of a measurement is

$$\text{relative error} = \frac{\text{greatest possible error}}{\text{measurement}},$$

often written as a percent.

### Example 2

Compare the relative errors of 7 cm and 250 cm, both measured to the nearest centimeter.

Both have GPE 0.5 cm. $\tfrac{0.5}{7} \approx 0.071 = 7.1\%$ and $\tfrac{0.5}{250} = 0.002 = 0.2\%$. The doorway measurement is far better, relative to its size, even though the ruler was the same.

When the true value is known (from a better instrument, or a definition), you can measure how far off a particular measurement actually was. The **[[percent error]]** is

$$\text{percent error} = \frac{|\text{measured} - \text{true}|}{\text{true}} \times 100\%.$$

### Example 3

A student measures a 50.0 cm board as 48.5 cm. What is the percent error?

$\dfrac{|48.5 - 50.0|}{50.0} \times 100\% = \dfrac{1.5}{50} \times 100\% = 3\%$.

## Errors grow in calculations

When you compute with measured values, their uncertainties carry into the answer, and multiplication makes them grow. The safe way to see how much is to compute with the bounds: the smallest possible answer from the lower bounds, the largest from the upper bounds.

### Example 4

A rectangle is measured as 8 cm by 5 cm, each to the nearest centimeter. Between what values does its true area lie? Its perimeter?

The length is between 7.5 and 8.5 cm; the width between 4.5 and 5.5 cm.

- Smallest area: $7.5 \times 4.5 = 33.75$ cm². Largest: $8.5 \times 5.5 = 46.75$ cm² (actually just under it).
- The calculated area, $8 \times 5 = 40$ cm², could be off by more than 6 cm²: about 16%, even though each side's relative error is only about 6% to 10%.
- Perimeter: from $2(7.5) + 2(4.5) = 24$ cm to $2(8.5) + 2(5.5) = 28$ cm, so $26 \pm 2$ cm.

The relative errors of the two sides roughly *add* when they are multiplied: $\tfrac{0.5}{8} \approx 6\%$ and $\tfrac{0.5}{5} = 10\%$, and the area's error is about $6\% + 10\% = 16\%$. (That shortcut is an approximation that works well when the errors are small.)

### Example 5

A cube's edge is measured as 10 cm to the nearest centimeter. Find the bounds on its volume.

Edge between 9.5 and 10.5 cm. Volume between $9.5^3 = 857.375$ and $10.5^3 = 1{,}157.625$ cm³. The calculated 1,000 cm³ could be off by about 15%: three factors each with a 5% relative error.

Volume multiplies three lengths together, so a small relative error in the length grows about three times over.

## Don't report more than you know

A calculator happily turns uncertain measurements into many digits. Reporting them all claims a precision you don't have.

### Example 6

A circular table's radius is measured as 4.2 ft, to the nearest tenth of a foot. Find its area and report it sensibly.

$A = \pi(4.2)^2 \approx 55.4177$ ft². The radius could be anywhere from 4.15 to 4.25 ft, so the area could be anywhere from $\pi(4.15)^2 \approx 54.1$ to $\pi(4.25)^2 \approx 56.7$ ft². Writing "55.4177 ft²" claims the area is known to a ten-thousandth of a square foot, when even the ones digit is uncertain by about 1. "About 55 ft²" is honest.

The significant-figures rule from the Module 6 honors lesson on significant figures (round a product or quotient to as many significant figures as the least precise measurement) gives the same answer here: 4.2 has two significant figures, so 55 ft². That rule is a quick shortcut; computing the bounds, as above, is the reliable check of how much an answer can be trusted.

## Common mistakes

- *Using the full precision as the error.* To the nearest centimeter, the GPE is 0.5 cm, not 1 cm.
- *Ignoring trailing zeros.* 12.00 s and 12 s are different measurements.
- *Mixing the bounds.* The smallest area comes from multiplying the two lower bounds, the largest from the two upper bounds.
- *Dividing by the wrong number in percent error.* Divide by the true value, not the measured one.
- *Reporting every calculator digit.* An answer can't be more precise than the measurements behind it.
- *Confusing precise with accurate.* A finely marked tool can still give wrong readings.

## Key points

- Precision: the unit a measurement was rounded to. Greatest possible error: half of it.
- A measurement $m$ with GPE $e$ lies between the lower bound $m - e$ and the upper bound $m + e$.
- Accuracy is closeness to the true value; precision is how finely the value is measured.
- Relative error $= \tfrac{\text{GPE}}{\text{measurement}}$; percent error $= \tfrac{|\text{measured} - \text{true}|}{\text{true}} \times 100\%$.
- Find bounds on an area or volume by computing with the lower bounds and with the upper bounds. Errors grow when measurements are multiplied.
- Round answers so they don't claim more precision than the measurements support.

lessons.title: Scaling area and volume
lessons.body:
## Bigger in every direction

Lesson 16 introduced the **[[scale factor]]**: the number you multiply every length by to go from one similar figure to another. A 1 : 24 model car has every length $\tfrac{1}{24}$ of the real one. This module has dropped hints that areas and volumes don't follow the same rule: in Lesson 33, doubling a pizza's radius gave *four* times the pizza, and in the honors lesson on spheres, doubling the radius multiplied the volume by 8. This lesson explains the pattern behind those hints, uses it on maps and models, runs it backwards, and ends with a surprising consequence for living things: why a giant ant could not simply be a big copy of a small one.

Throughout, $k$ is the scale factor for lengths, going from the original figure to the new one. If $k > 1$ the copy is an enlargement; if $0 < k < 1$ it is a reduction.

## Lengths scale by k

When a figure is scaled by $k$, *every* length is multiplied by $k$: not only the sides, but the perimeter, the diagonals, the height, the radius and the circumference. A rectangle 3 cm by 5 cm has perimeter 16 cm; scaled by $k = 2$ it is 6 cm by 10 cm with perimeter 32 cm, also twice as much. Angles don't change at all, which is why the copy has the same shape.

## Areas scale by k²

Area is counted in unit squares (Lesson 32). Scale a unit square by $k$ and its sides become $k$ long, so it becomes a $k \times k$ square, which holds $k^2$ unit squares.

![Three squares side by side. The first has side 1 and area 1. The second has side 2 and is divided into 4 unit squares, area 4. The third has side 3 and is divided into 9 unit squares, area 9. The heading says: lengths times k, so area times k squared; each unit square becomes k by k squares.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Any figure can be filled (exactly, or as closely as you like) with small squares. Scaling the figure scales every one of those little squares, and each one's area is multiplied by $k^2$, so the whole figure's area is multiplied by $k^2$:

$$\text{new area} = k^2 \times \text{old area}.$$

You can also see it in any formula. A rectangle's area $lw$ becomes $(kl)(kw) = k^2\,lw$; a circle's $\pi r^2$ becomes $\pi(kr)^2 = k^2\,\pi r^2$. Each area formula multiplies two lengths, so it picks up two factors of $k$. The number $k^2$ is the **[[area scale factor]]**.

### Example 1

A 4 in by 6 in photo is enlarged to 12 in by 18 in. How do its perimeter and area change?

The scale factor is $k = \tfrac{12}{4} = \tfrac{18}{6} = 3$. Perimeter: $20$ in becomes $60$ in, times 3. Area: $24$ in² becomes $216$ in², and $216 \div 24 = 9 = 3^2$. The enlargement needs 9 times as much paper and ink, not 3 times.

## Volumes scale by k³

Volume is counted in unit cubes (Lesson 34). Scale a unit cube by $k$ and it becomes a $k \times k \times k$ cube holding $k^3$ unit cubes.

![Three cubes. The first has edge 1 and volume 1. The second has edge 2 and is built from 8 unit cubes, volume 8. The third has edge 3 and is built from 27 unit cubes, volume 27. The heading says: lengths times k, so volume times k cubed; each unit cube becomes k by k by k cubes.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

The same filling argument gives

$$\text{new volume} = k^3 \times \text{old volume}.$$

In formulas, every volume multiplies three lengths: $lwh$ becomes $(kl)(kw)(kh) = k^3\,lwh$. The number $k^3$ is the **[[volume scale factor]]**. Anything that is proportional to volume scales by $k^3$ too: how much a container holds, and the weight of a solid object made of the same material. A solid's *surface* area is still an area, so it scales by $k^2$.

### Example 2

A box is 2 cm by 3 cm by 4 cm. A similar box has every edge doubled. Compare their volumes and surface areas.

Original: $V = 2 \cdot 3 \cdot 4 = 24$ cm³ and $SA = 2(6 + 8 + 12) = 52$ cm². New box, 4 cm by 6 cm by 8 cm: $V = 192$ cm³ and $SA = 2(24 + 32 + 48) = 208$ cm². Volume: $192 \div 24 = 8 = 2^3$. Surface area: $208 \div 52 = 4 = 2^2$. Same box, three different multipliers: 2 for the edges, 4 for the cardboard, 8 for what fits inside.

### Example 3

A solid chocolate bunny 10 cm tall weighs 100 g and is wrapped in 150 cm² of foil. A similar solid bunny is 15 cm tall. How much does it weigh, and how much foil does it need?

$k = \tfrac{15}{10} = 1.5$. Weight scales by $k^3 = 3.375$: $100 \times 3.375 = 337.5$ g. Foil scales by $k^2 = 2.25$: $150 \times 2.25 = 337.5$ cm². A bunny only half again as tall weighs more than three times as much.

## Which factor? A summary

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: Choosing the multiplier when a figure is scaled by k
  accDescr: First find the length scale factor k, new length divided by matching old length. Then ask what kind of quantity you want. A length, such as a side, perimeter, height or circumference, is multiplied by k. An area, such as a surface, paint, fabric or land on a map, is multiplied by k squared. A volume, such as capacity or the weight of a solid made of the same material, is multiplied by k cubed. An angle does not change.
  A["Find k = new length / matching old length"] --> B{"What are you finding?"}
  B --> L["Length (side, perimeter, height): times k"]
  B --> S["Area (surface, paint, land): times k squared"]
  B --> V["Volume (capacity, weight): times k cubed"]
  B --> N["Angle: no change"]
```

## Maps and models

A map, floor plan or model is a **[[scale drawing]]** (or scale model): every length is the real length times the same small factor. A **[[map scale]]** like 1 : 50,000 is a ratio of *lengths*: 1 cm on the map stands for 50,000 cm on the ground, which is 500 m or 0.5 km. Model trains in the popular HO scale are built at about 1 : 87, so a real 12 m railcar becomes a model about $1{,}200 \div 87 \approx 13.8$ cm long.

Because the scale is for lengths, areas need the square of it. On a 1 : 50,000 map, a 1 cm by 1 cm square stands for a 0.5 km by 0.5 km square of land: $1 \text{ cm}^2$ on the map is $0.5^2 = 0.25 \text{ km}^2$ on the ground.

### Example 4

On a 1 : 50,000 map, a park covers 6 cm². What is its real area?

Each map square centimeter is 0.25 km² of land, so the park is $6 \times 0.25 = 1.5$ km². The tempting wrong answer, $6 \times 0.5 = 3$ km², uses the length scale on an area.

In ratio form: the scale factor from map to ground is $k = 50{,}000$, so areas are multiplied by $k^2 = 2{,}500{,}000{,}000$; $6 \text{ cm}^2 \times 2.5 \times 10^9 = 1.5 \times 10^{10} \text{ cm}^2$, which is the same 1.5 km² (since $1 \text{ km} = 10^5$ cm, $1 \text{ km}^2 = 10^{10}$ cm²). Converting the scale to "1 cm : 0.5 km" first is usually easier.

## Going backwards: from area to length

Sometimes you know how the areas compare and need the lengths. Since the area ratio is $k^2$, the length ratio is its square root:

$$k = \sqrt{\text{area ratio}}, \qquad k = \sqrt[3]{\text{volume ratio}}.$$

A square with 4 times the area has sides $\sqrt4 = 2$ times as long; a similar solid with 27 times the volume (or, made of the same material, the weight) is $\sqrt[3]{27} = 3$ times as tall. Use the square root only for an area ratio and the cube root only for a volume ratio, and only for similar figures: a rectangle can have 4 times the area by being 4 times as long and no wider.

### Example 5

Two similar rectangles have areas 20 cm² and 45 cm². The smaller is 4 cm wide. How wide is the larger?

Area ratio: $\tfrac{45}{20} = \tfrac94$. Length ratio: $k = \sqrt{\tfrac94} = \tfrac32$. Width: $4 \times \tfrac32 = 6$ cm. Check: the widths' ratio squared is $\left(\tfrac64\right)^2 = \tfrac94$. ✓

### Example 6

International paper sizes are designed so that two sheets of A4 side by side make one sheet of A3: A3 has exactly twice the area of A4, and the two are similar. An A4 sheet is 210 mm by 297 mm. What scale factor turns A4 into A3, and how big is A3?

Area ratio 2, so $k = \sqrt2 \approx 1.414$. The A3 sheet is about $210 \times 1.414 \approx 297$ mm by $297 \times 1.414 \approx 420$ mm (its official size is 297 mm by 420 mm). This is why a photocopier's "A4 → A3" button is labeled 141%, and "A3 → A4" is 71% ($\tfrac{1}{\sqrt2} \approx 0.707$). Doubling the area takes only about 41% more length in each direction.

## The square-cube law

Put the two rules side by side. Scale something up by $k$ and its areas grow by $k^2$ but its volume grows by $k^3$, faster. This mismatch is called the **[[square-cube law]]**, and it explains a lot about the sizes of real things. (Galileo described it in 1638, in his book *Two New Sciences*, to explain why a giant animal's bones would need to be much thicker than a scaled-up small animal's.)

*Strength versus weight.* The strength of a bone or a muscle depends mainly on its **[[cross-sectional area]]**: the area of the cut you would see if you sliced straight across it. So strength scales by $k^2$. An animal's weight depends on its volume, which scales by $k^3$. The load on each square centimeter of bone is weight ÷ area, which scales by $\tfrac{k^3}{k^2} = k$.

### Example 7

A movie giant is an exact copy of a 1.8 m, 80 kg person, scaled up 10 times to 18 m tall. What happens to the load on the giant's leg bones?

$k = 10$. Weight: $80 \times 10^3 = 80{,}000$ kg. Cross-section of each bone: $10^2 = 100$ times as large. Load on each square centimeter of bone: $\tfrac{1{,}000}{100} = 10$ times as much. Bone has some safety margin, but nowhere near tenfold: the giant's legs would be likely to break when it tried to walk. A real animal that large needs much thicker legs for its height, which is what you see comparing an elephant's legs with a gazelle's.

The same reasoning is why a giant ant can't be a scaled-up ant: its thin legs would buckle. Insects also have a second problem: they get oxygen through tiny air tubes that reach their tissues, a system that works well over short distances but poorly over long ones. (Hundreds of millions of years ago some insects were much bigger, such as dragonfly-like insects with wingspans of roughly 65 to 70 cm; one leading explanation is that the air then held more oxygen.)

*Small things cool faster.* Heat escapes through an object's surface, but the heat it holds (or, in a warm-blooded animal, produces) depends on its volume. Compare the **[[surface-area-to-volume ratio]]** of cubes:

| Edge | Surface area | Volume | Surface area ÷ volume |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 cm | 6 cm² | 1 cm³ | 6 per cm |
| 2 cm | 24 cm² | 8 cm³ | 3 per cm |
| 10 cm | 600 cm² | 1,000 cm³ | 0.6 per cm |

For a cube with edge $s$ the ratio is $\tfrac{6s^2}{s^3} = \tfrac{6}{s}$: scaling by $k$ multiplies it by $\tfrac{k^2}{k^3} = \tfrac1k$. A small object has much more surface for each bit of its volume, so it loses (and gains) heat faster.

```plot
{"x": [0, 10], "y": [0, 12.5], "yAxisAt": "left", "xAxisAt": "bottom", "xLabel": "edge (cm)", "yLabel": "surface area ÷ volume (per cm)", "functions": [{"f": "6/x", "from": 0.6, "to": 8}], "points": [{"at": [1, 6], "label": "(1, 6)"}, {"at": [2, 3], "label": "(2, 3)"}, {"at": [6, 1], "label": "(6, 1)"}], "caption": "Surface area ÷ volume for a cube is 6 ÷ edge: bigger cubes have far less surface for each cubic centimeter"}
```

That is why chopped potatoes cool faster than a whole one, why crushed ice melts faster than a block, and why a mouse must eat far more food for its body weight than an elephant does, just to stay warm.

*Simplified:* real animals are not exact scaled copies of each other, bone strength depends on more than cross-sectional area, and measured patterns in animals (such as how energy use grows with body size) are close to, but not exactly, what this simple $k^2$-versus-$k^3$ reasoning predicts. The square-cube law explains the direction of the effect, not every detail.

## Common mistakes

- *Using $k$ for everything.* Doubling the lengths doubles the perimeter but quadruples the area and multiplies the volume by 8.
- *Using a map's length scale on an area.* On a 1 : 50,000 map, 1 cm² is 0.25 km², not 0.5 km².
- *Forgetting that surface area is an area.* A solid's surface scales by $k^2$, its volume by $k^3$.
- *Dividing an area ratio instead of taking its square root.* Similar figures with 9 times the area have sides 3 times as long, not 4.5 or 9.
- *Scaling figures that aren't similar.* The $k^2$ and $k^3$ rules need the same shape, with every length multiplied by the same $k$.
- *Weight from scale with a different material or a hollow object.* Weight scales by $k^3$ only for solid objects of the same material.

## Key points

- Scaling by $k$ multiplies every length by $k$, every area by $k^2$ and every volume by $k^3$; angles stay the same.
- Why: each unit square becomes $k \times k$ unit squares, and each unit cube becomes $k \times k \times k$ unit cubes.
- A map or model scale is a length ratio; square it for areas, cube it for volumes.
- Backwards: $k = \sqrt{\text{area ratio}}$ or $\sqrt[3]{\text{volume ratio}}$, for similar figures only.
- Square-cube law: when something is scaled up, its volume (and weight) grows faster than its areas (strength, surface). Big animals need thicker bones; small objects cool faster.

lessons.title: Mean, median, mode and range
lessons.body:
## Summarizing a list of numbers

A list of test scores, daily temperatures or house prices can be long and hard to take in. Statistics boils such a list down to a few numbers that describe it. The most common are a "typical" value, called a measure of center, and a measure of how spread out the values are. This lesson covers the three measures of center (mean, median, mode) and the simplest measure of spread (range), and when each one is the right choice.

A collection of numbers like this is called a **[[data set]]**, and each number in it is a data value.

## The mean

The **[[mean]]** (the everyday "average") is the sum of the values divided by how many there are:

$$\text{mean} = \frac{\text{sum of the values}}{\text{number of values}}$$

### Example 1

Find the mean of the quiz scores 8, 6, 10, 7, 9, 8.

Sum: $8 + 6 + 10 + 7 + 9 + 8 = 48$. There are 6 scores. Mean $= 48 \div 6 = 8$.

The mean is a *balance point*. If you place the values as weights on a number line, the mean is where it would balance. That's why the distances above the mean exactly cancel the distances below it: here the deviations are $0, -2, +2, -1, +1, 0$, which sum to zero.

![A number line drawn as a seesaw beam resting on a triangle at 8. Dots sit above it at 6, 7, two at 8, 9 and 10. The text says the distances below 8 add to 3 and the distances above 8 add to 3, so the beam balances at the mean, 8.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Because the mean uses every value, one unusually large or small value, an **[[outlier]]**, can pull it a long way. If a seventh quiz score of 0 is added (a missed quiz), the mean drops to $48 \div 7 \approx 6.9$, below five of the seven scores.

## The median

The **[[median]]** is the middle value when the data are put in order.

- With an odd number of values, it's the one in the middle.
- With an even number, it's the mean of the two middle values.

### Example 2

Find the median of 14, 3, 9, 21, 6.

Order them: 3, 6, 9, 14, 21. The middle (third of five) is 9.

### Example 3

Find the median of 8, 6, 10, 7, 9, 8.

Order: 6, 7, 8, 8, 9, 10. The two middle values are the third and fourth, 8 and 8. Median $= \tfrac{8 + 8}{2} = 8$.

The median isn't affected much by outliers. Add the 0 from before: 0, 6, 7, 8, 8, 9, 10. The median is still 8. That's why medians are used for things like home prices and incomes, where a few very large values would make the mean misleading.

## The mode

The **[[mode]]** is the value that occurs most often. In 6, 7, 8, 8, 9, 10 the mode is 8. A data set can have more than one mode (if two values tie for most frequent) or no mode (if every value appears once). The mode is the only measure of center that works for non-numerical data: if more people pick blue than any other color, blue is the mode.

## The range

The **[[range]]** is the difference between the largest and smallest values:

$$\text{range} = \text{maximum} - \text{minimum}$$

It's a quick measure of spread. For 6, 7, 8, 8, 9, 10 the range is $10 - 6 = 4$. Two data sets can have the same mean but very different ranges: 50, 50, 50 and 0, 50, 100 both have mean 50, with ranges 0 and 100.

## Working backward with the mean

Since mean = sum ÷ count, the sum is mean × count. This lets you find a missing value.

### Example 4

Kai's first four test scores are 82, 75, 90 and 88. What score does he need on the fifth test to have a mean of 85?

For a mean of 85 over 5 tests, the total must be $85 \times 5 = 425$. His current total is $82 + 75 + 90 + 88 = 335$. He needs $425 - 335 = 90$.

### Example 5

The mean of six numbers is 12. When a seventh number is added, the mean becomes 13. What is the seventh number?

Total of six: $6 \times 12 = 72$. Total of seven: $7 \times 13 = 91$. The new number is $91 - 72 = 19$.

## Choosing a measure

| Situation | Best measure of center |
|---|---|
| Values fairly symmetric, no outliers | mean |
| Outliers or a lopsided (skewed) data set | median |
| Categories, or "most popular" | mode |

The same choice as a flowchart:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: Choosing a measure of center
  accDescr: Start with the data to summarize. If the data are categories, such as favorite colors, use the mode. If the data are numbers, ask whether there are outliers or the data are lopsided. If yes, use the median; if no, use the mean. Either way, report a measure of spread such as the range along with the center.
  A[Data to summarize] --> B{"Numbers or categories?"}
  B -- Categories --> C[Use the mode]
  B -- Numbers --> D{"Outliers, or lopsided data?"}
  D -- Yes --> E[Use the median]
  D -- No --> F[Use the mean]
  E --> G["Also give a spread, such as the range"]
  F --> G
```

The picture below puts all four measures on one dot plot of the data 1, 7, 8, 9, 9, 10. The outlier, 1, drags the mean (about 7.3) to the left of the median (8.5), while the mode sits where the dots stack highest.

![A dot plot of 1, 7, 8, 9, 9, 10 on a number line from 0 to 11. The dot at 1 is marked as an outlier. A triangle under the line at about 7.3 marks the mean, and a diamond at 8.5 marks the median. The stack of two dots at 9 is the mode. A bracket above the dots from 1 to 10 shows the range, 9.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

### Example 6

Five employees earn \$38,000, \$41,000, \$43,000, \$45,000 and \$250,000 (the owner). Which better describes a typical salary, the mean or the median?

Mean: $(38 + 41 + 43 + 45 + 250) \div 5 = 417 \div 5 = 83.4$ thousand, or \$83,400, which is higher than four of the five salaries. Median: \$43,000, the middle value. The median is the better description; the owner's salary is an outlier.

## Common mistakes

- *Finding the median without ordering the values first.*
- *Forgetting to average the two middle values* when the count is even.
- *Dividing by the wrong count* for the mean, especially after adding or removing a value.
- *Reporting the range as two numbers* ("6 to 10"). The range is the single difference, 4.
- *Thinking the mean must be one of the data values.* It often isn't (the mean of 1, 2, 4 is $\tfrac73$).

## Key points

- Mean = sum ÷ count; it uses every value and is pulled by outliers.
- Median = middle value of the ordered data (average the two middle values for an even count); resistant to outliers.
- Mode = most frequent value; can be none or several.
- Range = maximum − minimum.
- Sum = mean × count, which lets you find a missing value.

lessons.title: Reading tables and graphs
lessons.body:
## Data you can see

Numbers in a long list are hard to compare at a glance. Tables organize them, and graphs turn them into pictures: you can see which bar is tallest or where a line rises fastest before reading a single number. This lesson covers the common displays (tables, bar graphs, line graphs and circle graphs), how to read values from them, and the calculations you'll often be asked to do with what you read: differences, totals, percents and percent change.

## Tables

A table arranges data in rows and columns. Always read the title, the row and column headings, and the units before reading any values.

| Month | Visitors | Revenue (dollars) |
|---|---|---|
| June | 1,240 | 9,920 |
| July | 1,860 | 14,880 |
| August | 1,550 | 12,400 |

### Example 1

Using the table, what was the mean revenue per visitor in July, and what was the percent increase in visitors from June to July?

Revenue per visitor in July: $14{,}880 \div 1{,}860 = 8$ dollars. Percent increase in visitors: $(1{,}860 - 1{,}240) \div 1{,}240 = 620 \div 1{,}240 = 0.5$, a 50% increase.

## Bar graphs

A **[[bar graph]]** compares amounts across categories using bars whose lengths are proportional to the amounts. Read a bar's value from where its top meets the scale on the vertical axis.

Every graph has the same working parts. Before reading any value, find each of them:

![A bar graph titled Favorite lunch with bars for Pizza 18, Tacos 12, Salad 6 and Soup 9. Lettered tags mark its parts: A the title, B the vertical axis label Number of students, C the scale 0 to 20 in steps of 5, D a bar, E a category label under a bar, and F the horizontal axis label Lunch choice.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

```plot
{"x": [0, 6], "y": [0, 50], "bars": [{"x": 1, "height": 35, "width": 0.7, "label": "Mon"}, {"x": 2, "height": 20, "width": 0.7, "label": "Tue"}, {"x": 3, "height": 45, "width": 0.7, "label": "Wed"}, {"x": 4, "height": 30, "width": 0.7, "label": "Thu"}, {"x": 5, "height": 40, "width": 0.7, "label": "Fri"}], "xLabel": "Day", "yLabel": "Books sold", "caption": "Books sold at a store, Monday to Friday"}
```

### Example 2

Using the bar graph: (a) How many more books were sold on Wednesday than on Tuesday? (b) What was the mean number sold per day?

(a) Wednesday 45, Tuesday 20: $45 - 20 = 25$ more.

(b) Total: $35 + 20 + 45 + 30 + 40 = 170$. Mean: $170 \div 5 = 34$ books per day.

*Watch the scale.* A vertical axis that doesn't start at zero exaggerates differences: if the axis ran from 15 to 50, Tuesday's bar would look a tiny fraction of Wednesday's even though Wednesday's value is a bit more than double. Always check where the scale starts.

![Two bar graphs of the same data, Tuesday 20 and Wednesday 45. On the left the scale starts at 0 and Wednesday's bar is a bit more than twice as tall as Tuesday's. On the right the scale starts at 15, so Tuesday's bar is very short and Wednesday's looks about six times as tall.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

On the right, Tuesday's bar shows only $20 - 15 = 5$ units and Wednesday's shows $45 - 15 = 30$, so Wednesday *looks* 6 times as big, though $45 \div 20 = 2.25$.

## Line graphs

A **[[line graph]]** shows how a quantity changes over time. Points are plotted for each time and connected by segments. A segment that rises shows an increase, a falling one a decrease, and a steeper segment a faster change.

