drills.solution: For a mean of {t} over 5 tests, the total must be {t} × 5 = {tot}. You have {a} + {b} + {c} + {d} = {have}. You need {tot} − {have} = **{need}**.

drills.title: Read a bar graph
drills.prompt: The bar graph shows cars washed at a car wash each week. Find the total for all four weeks, and how many more (negative for fewer) were washed in week 3 than in week 1.
drills.solution: Total: {a1} + {a2} + {a3} + {a4} = **{tot}**. Week 3 minus week 1: {a3} − {a1} = **{df}**.

drills.title: Read a circle graph
drills.prompt: A circle graph shows a company budget of {T:money0}. The marketing sector is {p}% of the budget. How many dollars go to marketing, and what is the angle of that sector?
drills.solution: Amount: {p}% of {T:money0} = {dp} × {T:int} = **{amt:money}**. Angle: {p}% of 360° = {dp} × 360° = **{ang}°**.

drills.title: Probability of drawing a color
drills.prompt: A bag holds {r} red, {b} blue and {g} green marbles. One is drawn at random. What is the probability it is blue? Give a fraction in lowest terms.
drills.solution: There are ${r} + {b} + {g} = {n}$ marbles, {b} of them blue. $P(\text{blue}) = \dfrac{{b}}{{n}} =$ **${P:texfrac}$**.

drills.title: Probability of a complement
drills.prompt: A bag holds {r} red, {b} blue and {g} green marbles. One is drawn at random. What is the probability it is NOT red? Give a fraction in lowest terms.
drills.solution: $P(\text{red}) = \dfrac{{r}}{{n}}$, so $P(\text{not red}) = 1 - \dfrac{{r}}{{n}} =$ **${P:texfrac}$**. (Or count directly: {b} + {g} non-red marbles out of {n}.)

drills.title: Two independent draws
drills.prompt: A jar holds {r} red and {b} blue chips. A chip is drawn, put back, and a second chip is drawn. What is the probability the first is red and the second is blue? Give a fraction in lowest terms.
drills.solution: The chip is replaced, so the draws are independent: $\dfrac{{r}}{{n}} \times \dfrac{{b}}{{n}} = \dfrac{{rb}}{{nn}} =$ **${P:texfrac}$**.

drills.title: Remainder of a product
drills.prompt: Without multiplying it out, find the remainder when {fa} × {fb} is divided by {md}.
drills.solution:
Replace each factor by its remainder. {fa} ÷ {md} leaves remainder {ra}, and {fb} ÷ {md} leaves remainder {rb}.

Multiply the remainders: ${ra} \times {rb} = {pr}$. Reduce again: ${pr} \div {md}$ leaves remainder **{ans}**.

drills.title: Last digit of a power
drills.prompt: What is the last digit of ${bs}^{ {ex} }$?
drills.solution:
Only the last digit of the base matters, and it is {ld}. The last digits of its powers cycle with length 4: {c1}, {c2}, {c3}, {c4}, then repeat.

Divide the exponent by 4: ${ex} = {qt} \times 4 + {rm}$. A remainder of {rm} points to position {pos} of the cycle (a remainder of 0 always points to the last position, 4).

The last digit is **{ans}**.

drills.title: Day of the week after many days
drills.prompt: Number the days of the week Sunday = 0, Monday = 1, …, Saturday = 6. Today is {dy}. What is the number of the day of the week {nd} days from today?
drills.solution:
Whole weeks don't change the day: ${nd} = {wk} \times 7 + {lft}$, so only the leftover days matter, and there are {lft} of them.

{dy} is day {dn}. Move forward {lft}: ${dn} + {lft} = {tot}$, and reducing by 7 if needed gives day **{ans}**.

drills.title: Consecutive whole numbers with a given sum
drills.prompt: The sum of {kk} consecutive whole numbers is {sm}. What is the largest of the numbers?
drills.solution:
Call the middle number $n$. The numbers are spread evenly around it ({half} below and {half} above), so the ones below and above cancel in pairs and the sum is ${kk}n$.

So ${kk}n$ equals {sm}, and dividing by {kk} gives $n = {mid}$. The largest is {half} more than the middle: ${mid} + {half} =$ **{big}**.

drills.title: Count the multiples in a range
drills.prompt: How many multiples of {kk} are there from {lo} to {hi}, including both ends?
drills.solution:
Multiples of {kk} from 1 to {hi}: the quotient of {hi} ÷ {kk} is {up}.

Leave out the ones below {lo}, that is, from 1 to {lom}: the quotient of {lom} ÷ {kk} is {below}.

Answer: {up} − {below} = **{ans}**.

drills.title: Divisible by one number or another

calc.ans: floor(top / na) + floor(top / nb) - floor(top / lcm(na, nb))

drills.prompt: How many whole numbers from 1 to {top} are divisible by {na} or by {nb} (or both)?
drills.solution:
Multiples of {na}: {ca}. Multiples of {nb}: {cb}.

Numbers divisible by both are the multiples of LCM({na}, {nb}) = {lc}: there are {cab}.

Inclusion–exclusion: {ca} + {cb} − {cab} = **{ans}**.

drills.title: Zeros at the end of a factorial
drills.prompt: How many zeros are at the end of {nn}! (that is, {nn} factorial, written out in full)?
drills.solution:
Each end zero needs a factor $10 = 2 \times 5$, and there are more 2s than 5s, so count the 5s.

Multiples of 5: {q1}. Multiples of 25 (a second 5 each): {q2}. Multiples of 125 (a third): {q3}. Multiples of 625 (a fourth): {q4}.

Total: ${q1} + {q2} + {q3} + {q4} =$ **{ans}** zeros.

drills.title: Count the terms of an arithmetic sequence
drills.prompt: How many numbers are in the list ${st}, {s2}, {s3}, \ldots, {lst}$, which goes up by {df} each time?
drills.solution:
From {st} to {lst} is ${lst} - {st} = {gap}$. Each step is {df}, so there are ${gap} \div {df} = {steps}$ steps.

There is one more number than steps (fence posts and gaps): ${steps} + 1 =$ **{nt}**.

drills.title: Sum of an arithmetic sequence
drills.prompt: Find the sum ${st} + {s2} + {s3} + \cdots + {lst}$. (It has {nt} terms.)
drills.solution:
Pair the first term with the last, the second with the second-to-last, and so on: each pair adds to ${st} + {lst} = {pairsum}$.

Sum $=$ number of terms $\times$ (first + last) $\div 2 = {nt} \times {pairsum} \div 2 =$ **{ans:int}**.

drills.title: Handshakes
drills.prompt: {pp} people at a meeting each shake hands once with every other person. How many handshakes are there?
drills.solution: Each person shakes {each} hands, giving {pp} × {each} = {dbl} hand-counts. Every handshake was counted twice (once for each person), so there are {dbl} ÷ 2 = **{ans:int}** handshakes.

drills.title: Convert from another base to base ten
drills.prompt: Convert ${d3}{d2}{d1}{d0}_{{b}}$ to base ten.
drills.solution:
In base {b} the places, from the right, are worth 1, {b}, {p2} and {p3}. Expanded form:
${d3} \times {p3} + {d2} \times {p2} + {d1} \times {b} + {d0} \times 1 = {t3} + {t2} + {t1} + {d0} =$ **{v}**.

drills.title: Write a number in binary
drills.prompt: Write {n} in binary (base two). Type only the digits 0 and 1.
drills.solution:
Divide by 2 repeatedly and read the remainders from last to first (or take out the biggest place value that fits, again and again). The binary places are 64, 32, 16, 8, 4, 2, 1, and
${n} = {b6} \times 64 + {b5} \times 32 + {b4} \times 16 + {b3} \times 8 + {b2} \times 4 + {b1} \times 2 + {b0} \times 1$,
so {n} in binary is **{bin:dp0}** (a leading 0 can be dropped).

drills.title: Convert hexadecimal to base ten
drills.prompt: Convert the hexadecimal number {h1}{h0} (base sixteen) to base ten.
drills.solution:
In hexadecimal, A = 10, B = 11, C = 12, D = 13, E = 14 and F = 15, and the places are 16 and 1.
The digit {h1} stands for {a1} and the digit {h0} stands for {a0}, so the value is ${a1} \times 16 + {a0} = {t1} + {a0} =$ **{v}**.

drills.title: GCF by the Euclidean algorithm
drills.prompt: Use the Euclidean algorithm to find the greatest common factor of {a:int} and {b:int}.
drills.solution:
Divide, then replace the pair with (divisor, remainder):
${a} = {q1} \times {b} + {r1}$, then ${b} = {q2} \times {r1} + {r2}$, and so on until a remainder is 0.
The last nonzero remainder is the GCF: **{f}**. (Check: ${a} = {f} \times {m}$ and ${b} = {f} \times {k}$, and {m} and {k} share no factor but 1.)

drills.title: LCM from the GCF
drills.prompt: The greatest common factor of {a:int} and {b:int} is {f}. Find their least common multiple.
drills.solution:
For two numbers, GCF × LCM = their product, so $\text{LCM} = \dfrac{{a} \times {b}}{{f}}$.
Divide first: ${a} \div {f} = {m}$, so $\text{LCM} = {m} \times {b} =$ **{l:int}**.

drills.title: Count divisors from the prime factorization
drills.prompt: How many divisors does {n:int} have? (Count 1 and {n:int} too.)
drills.solution:
Prime factorization: ${n} = 2^{{a}} \times 3^{{b}} \times 5^{{c}}$.
Add 1 to each exponent and multiply: ${a1} \times {b1} \times {c1} =$ **{cnt}** divisors.

drills.title: Lower and upper bounds for a product
drills.prompt: Round both factors down to the tens, and then both up to the tens, to find a lower bound and an upper bound for ${x} \times {y}$.
drills.solution:
Lower bound: ${xd} \times {yd} =$ **{lo:int}**. Upper bound: ${xu} \times {yu} =$ **{hi:int}**.
The exact product, {ex:int}, lies between them.

drills.title: Range of a rounded number
drills.prompt: A whole number rounds to {big:int} when it is rounded to the nearest {p}. What are the smallest and the largest whole numbers it could be?
drills.solution:
Halfway between multiples of {pv:int} is {half:int} away. Numbers from {half:int} below {big:int} (halfway rounds up) to one less than {half:int} above it round to {big:int}.
Smallest: **{lo:int}**. Largest: **{hi:int}**.

drills.title: Chain a rate through minutes, hours and days
drills.prompt: Something happens {r} times a minute. How many times does it happen in one {per}?
drills.solution:
An hour is 60 minutes, a day is $24 \times 60 = 1{,}440$ minutes and a week is $7 \times 1{,}440 = 10{,}080$ minutes.
One {per} is {mins:int} minutes, so the count is ${r} \times {mins} =$ **{ans:int}**.

drills.title: Multiply a negative by a number near 100
drills.prompt: Use the distributive property to find $\;({a})({n})$ without a calculator.
drills.solution: Write ${n} = 100 {sk:signed}$ and distribute: $({a})(100 {sk:signed}) = ({a})(100) + ({a})({sk}) = {h} + ({ask}) =$ **{v}**.

drills.title: Factor out a common negative
drills.prompt: Find $\;({a})({b}) + ({a})({c})$ by first factoring out the common factor ${a}$.
drills.solution:
Both products share the factor ${a}$, so $({a})({b}) + ({a})({c}) = ({a})\big({b} + ({c})\big) = ({a})({bc}) =$ **{v}**.
Check the long way: ${ab} {ac:signed} = {v}$.

drills.title: Solve an absolute value equation
drills.prompt: Solve $\;{m}|x {na:signed}| {k:signed} = {r}$. Enter both solutions.
drills.solution:
Isolate the absolute value. Undo the ${k:signed}$: ${m}|x {na:signed}| = {r} {nk:signed} = {md}$. Divide by {m}: $|x {na:signed}| = {d}$.
$|x {na:signed}|$ is the distance from $x$ to ${a}$, so $x = {a} - {d} =$ **{lo}** or $x = {a} + {d} =$ **{hi}**.

drills.title: Midpoint of two integers
drills.prompt: Find the midpoint of ${a}$ and ${b}$ on the number line.
drills.solution:
The distance is ${b} - ({a}) = {dist}$; half of it is {half}. Start at ${a}$ and move {half} to the right: ${a} + {half} =$ **{mid}**.
(Or average: $\dfrac{{sm}}{2} = {mid}$.)

drills.title: Count the integers within a distance
drills.prompt: How many integers $x$ satisfy $\;|x {na:signed}| {rel} {d}$?
drills.solution:
$|x {na:signed}|$ is the distance from $x$ to ${a}$. The numbers exactly {d} away are ${lo}$ and ${hi}$.
From ${lo}$ to ${hi}$ with both ends included there are ${hi} - ({lo}) + 1 = {all}$ integers. With $\le$ the ends count; with $<$ they are left out (subtract 2).
Answer: **{v}**.

drills.title: Simplify a complex fraction
drills.prompt: Simplify $\dfrac{1 + \tfrac{{a}}{{b}}}{1 - \tfrac{{c}}{{d}}}$. Give an exact fraction (improper is fine) or a whole number.
drills.solution: The LCD of {b} and {d} is {L}. Multiply every term on top and bottom by {L}, including the 1s: $\dfrac{{L} + {ta}}{{L} - {tc}} = \dfrac{{top}}{{bot}}$, which simplifies to **${v:texfrac}$**.

drills.title: Evaluate a continued fraction
drills.prompt: Evaluate $\;{a} + \cfrac{1}{{b} + \cfrac{1}{{c}}}$. Give an exact improper fraction or a mixed number.
drills.solution: Work from the bottom up. ${b} + \tfrac{1}{{c}} = \tfrac{{bc1}}{{c}}$. Flip it: $1 \div \tfrac{{bc1}}{{c}} = \tfrac{{c}}{{bc1}}$. Add {a}: **${v:texfrac}$**.

drills.title: Find the starting amount from what's left
drills.prompt: Rosa spent $\tfrac{{m}}{{p}}$ of her money on a concert ticket and then $\tfrac{1}{{q}}$ of what remained on dinner. She has {L} dollars left. How many dollars did she start with?
drills.solution: Fraction left after each step: $1 - \tfrac{{m}}{{p}}$, then $1 - \tfrac{1}{{q}}$ of that. Multiplied, the fraction of her money left is ${fl:texfrac}$. So ${fl:texfrac}$ of the start is {L}, and the start is ${L} \div {fl:texfrac} =$ **{S}** dollars. Check: the ticket costs {first}, leaving {rest}; dinner costs {second}, leaving {L}.

drills.title: Working together
drills.prompt: One machine can do a job alone in {ta} hours, and another can do it alone in {tb} hours. Working together at these rates, how many hours do they take? Give an exact fraction or a mixed number (for example 2 2/5).
drills.solution: Rates: $\tfrac{1}{{ta}} + \tfrac{1}{{tb}} = \tfrac{{den}}{{num}}$ job per hour. Time $= 1 \div \tfrac{{den}}{{num}} = \tfrac{{num}}{{den}}$ (product over sum), which is **${v:texfrac}$** hours.

drills.title: Average speed for a round trip
drills.prompt: A cyclist rides to a park at {sa} mph and returns along the same route at {sb} mph. What is the average speed for the round trip, in mph? Give an exact fraction, a mixed number or a whole number.
drills.solution: Equal distances, so use the harmonic mean: $\dfrac{2 \times {sa} \times {sb}}{{sa} + {sb}} = \dfrac{{num}}{{den}} =$ **${v:texfrac}$** mph. It is less than the plain average, {plain} mph, because more time is spent at the slower speed.

drills.title: Pure repeating decimal to a fraction
drills.prompt: Write $0.\overline{{d1}{d2}}$ as a fraction in lowest terms.
drills.solution:
Let $x = 0.\overline{{d1}{d2}}$. The repeating block has 2 digits, so multiply by 100: $100x = {n}.\overline{{d1}{d2}}$.
Subtract $x$ so the repeating tails cancel: $99x = {n}$, so $x = \dfrac{{n}}{99}$.
In lowest terms: **${val:texfrac}$**.

drills.title: Mixed repeating decimal to a fraction
drills.prompt: Write $0.{a}\overline{{b}}$ (only the {b} repeats) as a fraction in lowest terms.
drills.solution:
Let $x = 0.{a}\overline{{b}}$. Move the point just before the repeating part: $10x = {a}.\overline{{b}}$. Move it one more place (the period is 1): $100x = {ab}.\overline{{b}}$.
Subtract: $100x - 10x = {ab} - {a}$, so $90x = {n}$ and $x = \dfrac{{n}}{90}$.
In lowest terms: **${val:texfrac}$**.

drills.title: Inverse proportion (workers and days)
drills.prompt: {w1} workers can build a fence in {d1} days. Working at the same rate, how many days would {w2} workers take?
drills.solution:
Workers and days are inversely proportional: more workers, fewer days. The product stays the same: ${w1} \times {d1} = {t}$ worker-days.
So ${w2} \times d = {t}$, and $d = {t} \div {w2} =$ **{d2}** days.

drills.title: Workers, jobs and days
drills.prompt: {w1} painters paint {j1} rooms in {d1} days. Working at the same rate, how many painters are needed to paint {j2} rooms in {d2} days?
drills.solution:
Count the work in painter-days. So far: ${w1} \times {d1} = {tot}$ painter-days for {j1} rooms, which is ${tot} \div {j1} = {u}$ painter-days per room.
{j2} rooms need ${j2} \times {u} = {tot2}$ painter-days. Spread over {d2} days: ${tot2} \div {d2} =$ **{w2}** painters.

drills.title: Compound interest, yearly
drills.prompt: {prin:money0} is invested at {rate}% compounded yearly for {yrs} years. Find the balance at the end, to the nearest cent. (Don't round until the last step.)
drills.solution:
Use $A = P(1 + r)^t$. Write {rate}% as a decimal and add 1: the growth factor is {gf}.
${gf}^{{yrs}} \approx {pw:num4}$ (keep all the digits in the calculator), and {prin:money0} × {gf}^{yrs} ≈ {Aex:num4}, so the balance is **{bal:money}**.

drills.title: Compound interest, several times a year
drills.prompt: {prin:money0} is invested at {rate}% a year compounded {freq} for {yrs} years. Find the balance at the end, to the nearest cent. (Don't round until the last step.)
drills.solution:
Compounded {freq} means {per} periods a year. Each period pays {rate}% ÷ {per}, so each period multiplies the balance by $1 + \tfrac{{rate}/100}{{per}} \approx {gf:num4}$ (keep this unrounded in the calculator). There are {per} × {yrs} = {periods} periods.
$A = P\left(1 + \tfrac{r}{n}\right)^{nt}$ ≈ {Aex:num4}, so the balance is **{bal:money}**.

drills.title: Annual percentage yield
drills.prompt: An account pays {rate}% a year compounded {freq}. Find its annual percentage yield (APY) as a percent, to 2 decimal places.
drills.solution:
APY $= \left(1 + \tfrac{r}{n}\right)^n - 1$ with {per} periods a year. In one year the balance is multiplied by $\left(1 + \tfrac{{rate}/100}{{per}}\right)^{{per}} \approx {gfy:num4}$ (keep more digits in the calculator).
Subtract 1 and convert to a percent: APY ≈ {apy:num4}%, which is **{apy:num2}%** to 2 decimal places.

drills.title: Rule of 72
drills.prompt: Use the rule of 72 to estimate how many years it takes money to double at {rate}% interest compounded yearly.
drills.solution: Years to double ≈ 72 ÷ (rate as a percent) = 72 ÷ {rate} = **{dbl}** years. (The true doubling time is about {tru:num1} years; the rule is an estimate.)

drills.title: Depreciation at a fixed percent
drills.prompt: A vehicle bought for {prin:money0} loses {rate}% of its value each year. Using this model, find its value after {yrs} years, to the nearest cent.
drills.solution:
Each year it keeps {keep}% of its value, so multiply by {gf} once per year: $A = P(1 - r)^t$.
${gf}^{{yrs}} \approx {pw:num4}$, and {prin:money0} × {gf}^{yrs} ≈ {Aex:num4}, so the value is **{val:money}**.

drills.title: Net effect of two percent changes
drills.prompt: A price changes by {p1}%, and then the new price changes by {p2}% (a negative percent is a decrease). What is the overall percent change? Give the exact percent, negative for a decrease.
drills.solution: Multipliers: {m1} and {m2}. Their product is {m1} × {m2} = {mm:num4}. Overall change: ({mm:num4} − 1) × 100% = **{net}%**. (Adding the two percents would wrongly give {naive}%.)

drills.title: Undoing a percent change
drills.prompt: A price {dir} by {pct}%. By what percent must the new price change to return to the original price? Give the percent to 1 decimal place, negative for a decrease.
drills.solution: The first change multiplies the price by {m}. To undo it, multiply by 1 ÷ {m} ≈ {inv:num4}. As a percent change that is ({inv:num4} − 1) × 100% ≈ **{back:num1}%**.

drills.title: Percentage points and percent change
drills.prompt: An interest rate changes from {a:num1}% to {b:num1}%. Find the change in percentage points, and the percent change to 1 decimal place. Use negative numbers for decreases.
drills.solution:
Percentage points: subtract, {b:num1} − {a:num1} = **{pts:num1}** percentage points.
Percent change: divide the change by the original, {pts:num1} ÷ {a:num1} × 100% ≈ **{rel:num1}%**.

drills.title: Divide in scientific notation
drills.prompt: Divide and write the answer in scientific notation: $\;\dfrac{{a:num4} \times 10^{{m}}}{{q} \times 10^{{n}}}$
drills.solution:
Coefficients: ${a:num4} \div {q} = {quot:num4}$. Powers: $10^{{m} - ({n})} = 10^{{diff}}$.
If the coefficient is less than 1, move its point one place right and subtract 1 from the exponent. Answer: **${coef:num4} \times 10^{{ex}}$**.

drills.title: Simplest radical form
drills.prompt: Write $\sqrt{{n}}$ in simplest radical form, $a\sqrt{b}$.
drills.solution:
The largest perfect square that divides {n} is ${s}^2 = {sq}$: ${n} = {sq} \times {r}$, and {r} has no perfect-square factor other than 1.
So $\sqrt{{n}} = \sqrt{{sq}} \cdot \sqrt{{r}} =$ **${s}\sqrt{{r}}$**.

drills.title: Add or subtract square roots
drills.prompt: Simplify $\;\sqrt{{n1}} {sgn} \sqrt{{n2}}$ and write the answer as $a\sqrt{b}$ with $b$ as small as possible.
drills.solution:
Simplify each root: $\sqrt{{n1}} = {p}\sqrt{{k}}$ and $\sqrt{{n2}} = {q}\sqrt{{k}}$.
These are like radicals, so combine the coefficients: ${p} {sgn} {q} = {c}$, giving **${c}\sqrt{{k}}$**.

drills.title: Fractional exponents

choices.label: The exponent is positive, so that is the value.
The exponent is negative, so take the reciprocal.

drills.prompt: Evaluate $\;{base}^{{em}/{n}}$. Give an exact whole number or fraction.
drills.solution:
The denominator {n} means a root: $\sqrt[{n}]{{base}} = {r}$, because ${r}^{{n}} = {base}$. Then raise {r} to the power {m}, the size of the numerator: ${r}^{{m}} = {rm}$.
{sg} The answer is **{v:frac}**.

drills.title: Count significant figures
drills.prompt: How many significant figures does the measurement {x} have?
drills.solution:
Start counting at the first nonzero digit: leading zeros never count, zeros between nonzero digits always count, and trailing zeros count when there is a decimal point.
So {x} has **{sfc:int}** significant figures.

drills.title: Multiply measurements
drills.prompt: A rectangle measures {lg:num2} m by {wid:num1} m. Find its area in square meters, rounded to the correct number of significant figures.
drills.solution:
{lg:num2} has 3 significant figures and {wid:num1} has 2, so the product keeps 2.
${lg:num2} \times {wid:num1} = {area:num4}$, which rounds to **{area:sig2} m²**.

drills.title: Add measurements
drills.prompt: Three samples have masses {m1:num1} g, {m2:num2} g and {m3:dp3} g. Find the total mass, rounded to match the least precise measurement.
drills.solution: Exact sum: ${m1:num1} + {m2:num2} + {m3:dp3} = {tot:dp3}$ g. The least precise measurement, {m1:num1} g, is known only to the tenths place, so round the total to tenths: **{rnd:dp1} g**.

drills.title: Solve a system by substitution
drills.prompt: Solve the system: $\;y = {m:coef}x {b:signed}\;$ and $\;{a:coef}x {c:signedcoef}y = {d}$.
drills.solution:
The first equation gives $y$, so substitute $({m:coef}x {b:signed})$ for $y$ in the second: ${a:coef}x {c:signedcoef}({m:coef}x {b:signed}) = {d}$.
Distribute: ${a:coef}x {cm:signedcoef}x {cb:signed} = {d}$. Combine: ${k:coef}x {cb:signed} = {d}$, so ${k:coef}x = {dcb}$ and $x =$ **{x0}**.
Back-substitute: $y = {m}({x0}) + ({b}) =$ **{y0}**.

drills.title: Solve a system by elimination
drills.prompt: Solve the system: $\;{a1:coef}x {b1:signedcoef}y = {c1}\;$ and $\;{a2:coef}x {b2:signedcoef}y = {c2}$.
drills.solution:
Make the $x$-coefficients match: multiply the first equation by ${a2}$ and the second by ${a1}$:
$${p}x {q1:signedcoef}y = {r1} \qquad {p}x {q2:signedcoef}y = {r2}$$
Subtract the second from the first: ${dq:coef}y = {dr}$, so $y =$ **{y0}**.
Substitute into the first equation: ${a1:coef}x {b1y:signed} = {c1}$, so ${a1:coef}x = {c1b}$ and $x =$ **{x0}**.

drills.title: Solve an absolute value equation
drills.prompt: Solve $\;{k}|{a:coef}x {b:signed}| {e:signed} = {f}$. Give the smaller solution first.
drills.solution:
Isolate the absolute value. Subtract $({e})$: ${k}|{a:coef}x {b:signed}| = {kc}$. Divide by {k}: $|{a:coef}x {b:signed}| = {c}$.
Split into two equations: ${a:coef}x {b:signed} = {c}$ gives $x = {x2}$, and ${a:coef}x {b:signed} = {nc}$ gives $x = {x1}$.
Solutions: **{x1}** and **{x2}**.

drills.title: Compound inequality with a negative coefficient
drills.prompt: Solve $\;{lo} < {a}x {b:signed} \le {hi}$. The answer has the form $L \le x < U$. Give $L$ and $U$.
drills.solution:
Subtract $({b})$ from all three parts: ${lob} < {a}x \le {hib}$.
Divide all three parts by ${a}$. It is negative, so both symbols reverse: ${U} > x \ge {L}$.
Written from smallest to largest: ${L} \le x < {U}$, so $L =$ **{L}** and $U =$ **{U}**.

drills.title: Absolute value inequality (between)
drills.prompt: Solve $\;|{a}x {b:signed}| < {c}$. The answer has the form $L < x < U$. Give $L$ and $U$.
drills.solution:
"Less than" means between: ${nc} < {a}x {b:signed} < {c}$.
Subtract $({b})$ from all three parts: ${lo} < {a}x < {hi}$. Divide by {a} (positive, no flip): ${L} < x < {U}$.
So $L =$ **{L}** and $U =$ **{U}**.

drills.title: Line through two points
drills.prompt: Write the equation of the line through $({x1}, {y1})$ and $({x2}, {y2})$ in slope-intercept form, $y = mx + b$.
drills.solution:
Slope: $m = \dfrac{{y2} - ({y1})}{{x2} - ({x1})} = \dfrac{{dy}}{{dx}} = {m:texfrac}$.
Point-slope form with $({x1}, {y1})$: $y - ({y1}) = {m:texfrac}\,(x - ({x1}))$.
Distribute: $y - ({y1}) = {m:texfrac}x {mx1:signed}$, then add $({y1})$ to both sides: **$y = {m:texfrac}x {b0:signed}$**.

drills.title: Perpendicular line through a point
drills.prompt: Write the equation of the line through $({p}, {q})$ that is perpendicular to $\;y = {m0:texfrac}x {b:signed}$. Use slope-intercept form.
drills.solution:
The given line has slope ${m0:texfrac}$. A perpendicular slope is its negative reciprocal: flip it and change the sign, giving ${n:texfrac}$.
Point-slope form through $({p}, {q})$: $y - ({q}) = {n:texfrac}\,(x - ({p}))$.
Distribute: $y - ({q}) = {n:texfrac}x {sk:signed}$, then add $({q})$ to both sides: **$y = {n:texfrac}x {B:signed}$**.

drills.title: Interior angle sum of a polygon
drills.prompt: Find the sum of the interior angles of a convex polygon with {n} sides.
drills.solution: Diagonals from one vertex cut it into $n - 2 = {t}$ triangles, so the angle sum is ${t} \times 180° =$ **{S:int}°**.

drills.title: Angles of a regular polygon
drills.prompt: A regular polygon has {n} sides. Find the measure of each exterior angle and of each interior angle.
drills.solution:
The exterior angles add to 360°, so each is $360° \div {n} =$ **{ext}°**. Each interior angle is $180° - {ext}° =$ **{inn}°**.
(Check: the interior angles add to ({n} − 2) × 180° = {S:int}°, and {S:int}° ÷ {n} = {inn}°.)

drills.title: Number of sides from an angle
drills.prompt: Each interior angle of a regular polygon measures {ang}°. How many sides does it have?
drills.solution: Each exterior angle is $180° - {ang}° = {ext}°$. The exterior angles add to 360°, so there are $360 \div {ext} =$ **{n}** sides.

drills.title: Volume of a cone
drills.prompt: A cone has radius {r} cm and height {h} cm. Find its volume to the nearest tenth (or type an exact answer like 12pi).
drills.solution: $V = \tfrac13 \pi r^2 h = \tfrac13 \pi ({r2})({h}) = {c:dp0}\pi \approx$ **{V:dp1} cm³**.

drills.title: Volume and surface area of a sphere
drills.prompt: A sphere has a {given} of {m} cm. Find its volume and its surface area, each to the nearest tenth (or type exact answers like 36pi).
drills.solution:
The radius is {r} cm. $V = \tfrac43 \pi r^3 = \tfrac43 \pi ({r3}) = {cv:dp0}\pi \approx$ **{V:dp1} cm³**.
$SA = 4\pi r^2 = 4\pi({r})^2 = {cs:dp0}\pi \approx$ **{S:dp1} cm²**.

drills.title: Slant height and lateral area of a cone
drills.prompt: A cone has radius {r} cm and height {h} cm. Find its slant height, and the area of its curved (lateral) surface to the nearest tenth (or exact, like 65pi).
drills.solution:
The radius, height and slant height form a right triangle with $\ell$ as the hypotenuse: $\ell^2 = {r2:dp0} + {h2:dp0} = {l2:dp0}$, so $\ell =$ **{l} cm**.
Lateral area $= \pi r \ell = \pi({r})({l}) = {c:dp0}\pi \approx$ **{L:dp1} cm²**.

drills.title: Bounds of a measurement

choices.label: the nearest tenth of a centimeter

drills.prompt: A length is measured as {m:num4} cm, to {p}. Find the greatest possible error, and the lower and upper bounds of the true length.
drills.solution:
The precision is {p:num4} cm, so the greatest possible error is half of it: **{e:num4} cm**.
Lower bound: {m:num4} − {e:num4} = **{lo:num4} cm**. Upper bound: {m:num4} + {e:num4} = **{hi:num4} cm**.

drills.title: Bounds on a rectangle's area
drills.prompt: A rectangle is measured as {l} m by {w} m, each to the nearest meter. Find the smallest and largest possible values of its true area.
drills.solution: Each side could be off by up to 0.5 m. Smallest: {l1} × {w1} = **{amin} m²**. Largest: {l2} × {w2} = **{amax} m²** (the true area is just under this). The calculated area, {A} m², lies between them.

drills.title: Percent error
drills.prompt: An object with a true mass of {t} g is measured as {meas} g. What is the percent error, to the nearest tenth of a percent?
drills.solution: Percent error $= \dfrac{|\text{measured} - \text{true}|}{\text{true}} \times 100\% = \dfrac{{d}}{{t}} \times 100\% \approx$ **{pe:dp1}%**.

drills.title: Mean absolute deviation
drills.prompt: Find the mean and the mean absolute deviation (MAD) of {a}, {b}, {c}, {d}, {e}.
drills.solution:
Mean: ({a} + {b} + {c} + {d} + {e}) ÷ 5 = {s} ÷ 5 = **{m}**.
Distances from the mean: |{a} − {m}| = {da}, |{b} − {m}| = {db}, |{c} − {m}| = {dc}, |{d} − {m}| = {dd}, |{e} − {m}| = {de}. They add to {sd}.
MAD = {sd} ÷ 5 = **{mad}**.

drills.title: Quartiles and the IQR
drills.prompt: Find Q1, Q3 and the interquartile range of these 9 values: {x4}, {x9}, {x1}, {x6}, {x3}, {x8}, {x2}, {x7}, {x5}. (Use the median-of-halves method: leave the median out of both halves.)

drills.title: Outlier fences
drills.prompt: A data set has Q1 = {q1} and Q3 = {q3}. Find the lower and upper fences of the 1.5 × IQR rule, and decide whether a value of {big} is flagged as an outlier (enter 1 for yes, 0 for no).
drills.solution:
IQR = {q3} − {q1} = {iqr}, and 1.5 × {iqr} = {step}.
Lower fence: {q1} − {step} = **{lo}**. Upper fence: {q3} + {step} = **{hi}**.
{big} is compared with the upper fence {hi}: the answer is **{out}** (1 means it is above the fence and flagged; 0 means it is not).

drills.title: Two draws without replacement
drills.prompt: A bag holds {r} red and {b} blue marbles. Two are drawn without replacement. Find the probability that both are red, and the probability of one of each color. Give fractions in lowest terms.
drills.solution:
There are {n} marbles. Both red: $\dfrac{{r}}{{n}} \times \dfrac{{r1}}{{n1}} = \dfrac{{rr}}{{tot}} =$ **${Pboth:texfrac}$**.
One of each: red then blue is $\dfrac{{r}}{{n}} \times \dfrac{{b}}{{n1}}$ and blue then red is $\dfrac{{b}}{{n}} \times \dfrac{{r}}{{n1}}$, each $\dfrac{{rb}}{{tot}}$. Add the two paths: $\dfrac{{rb2}}{{tot}} =$ **${Pmix:texfrac}$**.

drills.title: At least one, without replacement
drills.prompt: A box of {n} batteries contains {d} dead ones. Two batteries are chosen at random without replacement. What is the probability that at least one of them is dead? Give a fraction in lowest terms.
drills.solution:
Use the complement, "none dead." There are {g} good batteries: $P(\text{none}) = \dfrac{{g}}{{n}} \times \dfrac{{g1}}{{n1}} = \dfrac{{gg}}{{tot}} = {Pnone:texfrac}$.
So $P(\text{at least one dead}) = 1 - {Pnone:texfrac} =$ **${P:texfrac}$**.

drills.title: Expected value of a dice game
drills.prompt: A game costs {c:money0} to play. You roll a fair die: a 6 pays {w6:money0}, a 4 or a 5 pays {w45:money0}, and anything else pays nothing. Find the expected prize and the expected net gain per play (negative for a loss).
drills.solution:
Expected prize: ${w6} \cdot \tfrac16 + {w45} \cdot \tfrac26 + 0 \cdot \tfrac36 = \tfrac{{w6} + {two}}{6} = \tfrac{{tw}}{6}$, which is **{ev:money}**.
Expected net gain: {ev:money} − {c:money0} = **{net:money}** per play. (A value of 0 would make the game fair.)

drills.title: Surface area and volume of a scaled solid
drills.prompt: A solid has a surface area of {S0} cm² and a volume of {V0} cm³. A similar solid has every length multiplied by {k}. Find its surface area and its volume.
drills.solution:
The length scale factor is $k = {k}$. Surface area is an area, so it is multiplied by $k^2 = {k2:num4}$: ${S0} \times {k2:num4} =$ **{S:num4} cm²**.
Volume is multiplied by $k^3 = {k3:num4}$: ${V0} \times {k3:num4} =$ **{V:num4} cm³**.

drills.title: Real area from a map
drills.prompt: On a map with scale {sc}, a forest covers {m} cm². What is the real area of the forest, in square kilometers?
drills.solution:
1 cm on the map is {sc:int} cm on the ground. Since 1 km = 100,000 cm, that is {km:num4} km.
So 1 cm² on the map stands for ${km:num4} \times {km:num4} = {km2:num4}$ km² (square the length scale for an area).
The forest: ${m} \times {km2:num4} =$ **{A:num4} km²**.

drills.title: Length from an area ratio
drills.prompt: Two similar rectangles have areas {A1} cm² and {A2} cm². The smaller one is {L1} cm wide. How wide is the larger one?
drills.solution:
Area ratio: $\dfrac{{A2}}{{A1}} = \dfrac{{b2}}{{a2}}$. Lengths scale by the square root of the area ratio: $k = \sqrt{\dfrac{{b2}}{{a2}}} = \dfrac{{b}}{{a}}$.
Width: ${L1} \times \dfrac{{b}}{{a}} =$ **{L2} cm**.
